questions.question:
Fig. 10.1 shows apparatus for electrolysis of concentrated aqueous hydrochloric acid using carbon electrodes X and Y.
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
Write half equations, with state symbols, for the reactions at electrodes X and Y.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 3 MARKS
The gas discharged at electrode Y is bubbled into aqueous potassium iodide; with the aid of a chemical equation, describe and explain what would be observed.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
After some time, a new product was observed forming at electrode Y; state its identity and explain why it forms.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D) · 3 MARKS
In a separate experiment, copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed using copper electrodes. Student A says the colour intensity of the blue solution remains unchanged; Student B says it fades. Which student is correct? Explain with the help of half equations.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
B1
2H+(aq) + 2e- -> H2(g)
B2
2Cl-(aq) -> Cl2(g) + 2e-
PART (B) · 3 MARKS
B1
The colourless solution turns brown (iodine formed); a black solid may form if iodine is in excess.
B2
Cl2 + 2I- -> I2 + 2Cl- (or Cl2 + 2KI -> I2 + 2KCl)
B3
Chlorine is more reactive (more electronegative / higher oxidising power) than iodine, so it displaces iodine from potassium iodide.
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
B1
Oxygen gas
B2
As the concentration of chloride ions decreases (they are used up), hydroxide ions are preferentially discharged at the anode instead, forming oxygen.
PART (D) · 3 MARKS
B1
Student A is correct; at the anode, Cu(s) -> Cu2+(aq) + 2e- (the copper electrode dissolves, adding Cu2+ ions).
B2
Cu2+(aq) + 2e- -> Cu(s) (copper(II) ions are removed from solution and deposited as copper at the cathode).
B3
Since Cu2+ ions are added at the anode at the same rate as they are removed at the cathode, the concentration of Cu2+ ions (and the intensity of the blue colour) remains unchanged.

questions.question:
Potassium chlorate(V), KClO3, is a white crystalline solid at room conditions.
It decomposes to form potassium chloride and oxygen when heated to 400 degC in the presence of a catalyst, copper(II) oxide: 2KClO3 --CuO--> 2KCl + 3O2.
Table 10.1: melting points (degC) KClO3=368, KCl=770, CuO=1326; boiling points (degC) KClO3=not given, KCl=1420, CuO=2000; solubility in water: KClO3 soluble, KCl soluble, CuO insoluble.
PART (A) · 1 MARK
Suggest why the boiling point of potassium chlorate(V) is not given in Table 10.1
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 1 MARK
What is the physical state of potassium chlorate(V) when it starts to decompose (decomposes at 400 degC; m.p. = 368 degC)?
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
Describe briefly how you would obtain pure potassium chloride from a mixture of potassium chlorate(V), potassium chloride and copper(II) oxide.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D) · 1 MARK
State the oxidation state of chlorine in KClO3.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
Explain, in terms of oxidation number, why the decomposition of potassium chlorate(V) is a redox reaction.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (F) · 2 MARKS
With the aid of an equation, name a reaction that is not a redox reaction.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
KClO3 decomposes before it reaches its boiling point, so the boiling point cannot be measured/does not apply.
PART (B) · 1 MARK
B1
Liquid (400 degC is above the melting point of 368 degC).
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
B1
Heat the solid mixture (to ~400 degC) to decompose the KClO3 into KCl. Cool, weigh, then reheat and reweigh repeatedly until a constant mass is obtained, showing decomposition is complete.
B2
Add excess distilled water to the cooled solid mixture to dissolve the KCl. Filter to remove the insoluble CuO as the residue (KCl passes through in the filtrate).
B3
Heat the filtrate (containing KCl) to saturation. Cool to allow KCl crystals to form. Filter to collect the crystals. Wash with a little cold distilled water and dry between filter papers.
PART (D) · 1 MARK
B1
+5
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
B1
Chlorine's oxidation state decreases from +5 in KClO3 to -1 in KCl, so chlorine is reduced.
B2
Oxygen's oxidation state increases from -2 in KClO3 to 0 in O2 (its elemental form), so oxygen is oxidised. Since both oxidation (of O) and reduction (of Cl) occur, the reaction is redox.
PART (F) · 2 MARKS
B1
Neutralisation (acid + base -> salt + water), e.g. NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O. (Or: precipitation, e.g. AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3.)
B2
NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O (neutralisation), or AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3 (precipitation).

questions.answer:

PART (A) · 2 MARKS
B1
Each C atom in graphite forms only 3 covalent bonds to other C atoms, leaving 1 valence electron per atom that is not used in bonding
B2
The delocalised electrons are free to move throughout the graphite structure and act as mobile charge carriers, allowing current to flow and closing the circuit

questions.question:
Lead is extracted by heating its oxide with hydrogen: PbO + H2 -> Pb + H2O, using apparatus with hydrogen passed in excess over heated PbO, excess hydrogen burnt off, with fused calcium chloride as drying agent (Fig 5.1).
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
Is hydrogen acting as the oxidising agent or reducing agent? Explain using loss/gain of oxygen.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
'Aluminium can be extracted from its oxide using the same method.' Do you agree? Explain.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(III) · 2 MARKS
Explain why the flow of hydrogen gas must be maintained until the solid has completely cooled to room temperature
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 2 MARKS
A disproportionation reaction is one where the same element is both oxidised and reduced, forming two separate products, e.g. 4H3PO3 -> 3H3PO4 + PH3. Explain, in terms of oxidation states, why this is a disproportionation reaction.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 1 MARK
A comproportionation reaction also involves oxidation and reduction of the same element, e.g. 2H2S + SO2 -> 3S + 2H2O. Suggest how comproportionation reactions generally differ from disproportionation reactions.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Hydrogen is the reducing agent; it removes oxygen from PbO (PbO loses oxygen) to form Pb.
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
No — aluminium is more reactive than hydrogen (above hydrogen in the reactivity series), so hydrogen cannot remove oxygen from/reduce aluminium oxide; aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of molten Al2O3 instead.
PART (A)(III) · 2 MARKS
B1
The lead formed is still very hot when heating stops.
B2
Continued hydrogen flow keeps air/oxygen away from the hot lead so it does not react with oxygen and re-form lead(II) oxide.
PART (B)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
Oxidation state of P: +3 in H3PO3, +5 in H3PO4, -3 in PH3.
B2
P is oxidised (+3 -> +5, forming H3PO4) and P is reduced (+3 -> -3, forming PH3); since the same element is both oxidised and reduced, this is a disproportionation reaction.
PART (B)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
Comproportionation: two reactants (same element, different oxidation states) combine to give one product; disproportionation: one reactant splits into two separate products of that element.

questions.question:
Aqueous thiosulfate, S2O32-(aq), reacts with aqueous iodine: I2(aq) + 2S2O32-(aq) -> 2I-(aq) + S4O62-(aq). In a titration, 50.0 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 aqueous thiosulfate was added to 40 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 aqueous iodine.
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
Determine the limiting reagent. Show your workings clearly.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
Calculate the percentage yield of iodide ions if only 0.0013 mol of iodide ions were produced at the end of the experiment.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
Explain, in terms of oxidation states, why the aqueous thiosulfate acts as a reducing agent in this reaction.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D) · 1 MARK
Explain whether this reaction can be considered a disproportionation reaction.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
B1
moles S2O3^2- = 50.0/1000 dm3 x 0.1 mol/dm3 = 0.005 mol; moles I2 = 40.0/1000 dm3 x 0.1 mol/dm3 = 0.004 mol
B2
using the ratio S2O3^2- : I2 = 2:1, 0.005 mol S2O3^2- requires 0.005/2 = 0.0025 mol I2
B3
S2O3^2- (thiosulfate) is the limiting reagent, since the available I2 (0.004 mol) exceeds the 0.0025 mol needed to react with all the thiosulfate
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
M1
theoretical moles of I- = moles of limiting reagent (S2O3^2-) x (2/2) = 0.005 mol, using the 1:1 ratio S2O3^2- : I-
A1
% yield = (0.0013 mol / 0.005 mol) x 100% = 26.0%
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
B1
the oxidation state of iodine decreases (iodine is reduced) — since thiosulfate causes this reduction, and is itself oxidised, it is the reducing agent
B2
oxidation state of iodine: 0 in I2, -1 in I- (a decrease of 1); a reducing agent is itself oxidised while causing another species to be reduced
PART (D) · 1 MARK
B1
No — disproportionation requires the SAME element to be simultaneously oxidised and reduced; here iodine is reduced while sulfur (in thiosulfate) is oxidised, so two different elements are involved, not one

Membrane cell: ion-exchange polymer membrane allows only cations through; gives 33% NaOH directly.
Cl2 mixed with H2 explodes on exposure to sunlight/heat, forming HCl.
Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaOCl + H2O (disproportionation).

Draw it

B1
Oxygen
B2

B1

questions.question:
Passage on how CO2 affects the oceans.
CO2(aq) + H2O(l) <=> H2CO3(aq); H2CO3(aq) <=> HCO3-(aq) + H+(aq); CO32-(aq) + H+(aq) <=> HCO3-(aq).
A Bjerrum plot (Fig 8.1) shows % of each carbon-containing species vs pH.
Ocean surface pH has fallen from 8.2 to 8.1 in 200 years (~30% increase in acidity).
The Equatic-1 facility (Singapore) uses electrolysis of seawater to remove CO2: seawater enters cathode and anode chambers and is electrolysed into O2 and H2; at the cathode, pH rises and metal carbonates precipitate on a porous electrode (used in construction); the anode has an oxygen-evolution-selective coating; acidified seawater from the anode is neutralised by dissolving alkaline rocks (forsterite Mg2SiO4, anorthite CaAl2Si2O8) before release.
Table 8.3 gives seawater ion concentrations (mg/dm3): Na+ 10600, Mg2+ 1260, Ca2+ 400, K+ 380; Cl- 19000, SO4(2-) 2650, HCO3- 140, Br- 65.
A silicate anion has general formula [SiO(4-x)](4-2x)-]n, n a whole number, 0<=x<2.
PART (A) · 1 MARK
Based on Fig 8.1, arrange in increasing order the percentage of CO2(aq), HCO3-(aq) and CO32-(aq) in naturally-occurring seawater (pH ~8.2).

Draw it

Draw it

Draw it

Attach photo or sketch
Draw it

B1

2H+(aq) + 2e- -> H2(g)
B2

B2

H2 gas is used as a fuel that produces only water, eliminating further CO2 emissions and reducing reliance on fossil fuels

CO2 is removed from seawater as it is precipitated out as solid metal carbonates (CaCO3/MgCO3)

Bubbling air through the seawater removes CO2 from the atmosphere as dissolved HCO3-, re-establishing carbon levels and counteracting ocean acidification / restoring the ocean's capacity to absorb CO2

Electrolysis is energy intensive and may require fossil fuels to generate the electricity, adding more CO2 to the environment (unless powered by renewable/solar energy)

the copper brush is oxidised (Cu -> Cu2+ + 2e-) and gradually dissolves away, whereas platinum is chemically inert/unreactive and is not oxidised, so it does not dissolve and never needs replacing

questions.question:
Brine is a saturated NaCl solution (about 25% by mass NaCl).
Industrial electrolysis of brine can be carried out in a diaphragm cell (Fig. 10.1) or a membrane cell (Fig. 10.2).
In the diaphragm cell, brine is in the anode compartment (graphite or titanium electrode, graphite preferred); at the cathode, hydroxide ions and hydrogen gas form by reduction of water; NaCl gradually flows from anode to cathode compartment (no backflow of Na+).
If Cl2 and NaOH contact, Cl2 forms ClO-, ClO3- and Cl- ions.
In the membrane cell, brine is fed to a brine concentrator; current splits aqueous NaCl into Na+ and Cl-; Na+ flows through an ion-exchange membrane and reacts with OH- (from reduction of water) to form aqueous NaOH; without the membrane, the NaOH would be impure (would contain Cl-).

Global Warming Potential (GWP) compares warming impact to CO2 over 100 years.
Table 8.1 gives ODP/GWP for CFC-11 (CCl3F, ODP 1.00, GWP 4000), CFC-12 (CCl2F2, ODP 0.82, GWP 8500), CFC-113 (C2F3Cl3, ODP 0.90, GWP 11700), CFC-114 (structure unknown, ODP 0.85, GWP 5000).
Table 8.2 gives HCFC-22 (CHClF2, ODP 0.04, GWP 1700), an unnamed HCFC (C2HCl2F3, ODP 0.014, GWP 93), HFC-23 (CHF3, ODP < 4e-4, GWP 12100), HFC-125 (structure unknown, ODP < 3e-5, GWP 3200).
Naming follows the 'rule of 90': add 90 to the CFC number to get a 3-digit code where digit 1 = number of C atoms, digit 2 = number of H atoms, digit 3 = number of F atoms (remaining bonds are C-Cl).
CFCs break down ozone: sunlight breaks a C-Cl bond in CFC producing a Cl atom (e.g.
CCl3F -> CCl2F + Cl); Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2; ClO + O3 -> Cl + 2O2.
Bond energies: C-Cl = 328 kJ/mol, C-F = 485 kJ/mol, C-H = 413 kJ/mol.

Sunlight breaks the C-Cl bond in the CFC, releasing a Cl atom which reacts with O3 to form ClO + O2.

[Section B — answer ONE of Q9/Q10] Butene is an unsaturated hydrocarbon formed from catalytic cracking of diesel and lubricating oil fractions, an important petrochemical feedstock.
Fig. 9.1 shows the structure of butene.
Hydration of butene produces two isomeric alcohols.
Fig. 9.2 shows the structure of 1,3,5-hexatriene; when 20.0 kg of 1,3,5-hexatriene is hydrogenated, 21.0 kg of product is formed.
PART (A) · 1 MARK
Explain why butene is described as unsaturated.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 1 MARK
Describe what happens during cracking of petroleum fractions such as diesel and lubricating oil.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(I) · 2 MARKS
State the conditions required for the hydration of butene to form alcohols.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(II) · 2 MARKS
Draw the full structural formula of the two isomeric alcohols formed by hydration of butene.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(I) · 2 MARKS
Show, by calculation, that the product (21.0 kg) formed from hydrogenating 20.0 kg of 1,3,5-hexatriene is still unsaturated.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(II) · 2 MARKS
Describe a simple experiment to identify which of two 50 cm3 beakers contains 1,3,5-hexatriene and which contains the hydrogenated product from (d)(i).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
Butene contains a C=C double bond (it is an alkene).
PART (B) · 1 MARK
B1
Long-chain (large) hydrocarbon molecules are broken down (split) into shorter-chain (smaller) hydrocarbon molecules, using a catalyst and heat.
PART (C)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
300°C
B2
60 atm
B3
phosphoric(V) acid catalyst, H3PO4
PART (C)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-OH (butan-1-ol)
B2
CH3-CH2-CH(OH)-CH3 (butan-2-ol)
PART (D)(I) · 2 MARKS
M1
Mr(C6H8) = 6(12)+8(1) = 80; Mr(C6H14) = 6(12)+14(1) = 86; expected mass if fully saturated = (86/80) x 20.0 = 21.5 kg
B1
21.0 kg (actual) is less than 21.5 kg (mass expected if fully saturated); hence not all double bonds have been hydrogenated and the product is still unsaturated.
PART (D)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
Pipette 25.0 cm3 of each compound into a conical flask; titrate with aqueous bromine from a burette, adding until a permanent orange/brown colour just persists; record the volume of bromine water used for each.
B2
The compound requiring a larger volume of bromine water to give a permanent orange/brown colour is 1,3,5-hexatriene, since it has more C=C double bonds (is more unsaturated) than the hydrogenated product.
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
Table 10.1 shows the formulae of the first three members of the alcohol homologous series: methanol CH3OH, ethanol C2H5OH, propanol C3H7OH.
Ethanol can be manufactured from either ethene or glucose (fermentation): C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2.
Propanol reacts in a similar way to ethanol.
PART (A) · 1 MARK
State the general formula of the alcohol homologous series.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 2 MARKS
Write an equation for the production of ethanol from ethene, and state the conditions under which the reaction is carried out.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 3 MARKS
3.6 kg of glucose was fermented and 1.5 kg of ethanol was obtained. Calculate the percentage yield of ethanol. (C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2)
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(III) · 2 MARKS
Explain why ethanol made from ethene is a non-renewable fuel but ethanol made from glucose is a renewable fuel.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(I) · 1 MARK
Name the organic product formed when propanol reacts with warm, acidified potassium manganate(VII).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(II) · 1 MARK
Give the structure of the compound formed when the product in (c)(i) reacts with ethanol.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
CnH2n+1OH (equivalently CnH2n+2O)
PART (B)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH
B2
High temperature (about 300 degC) and high pressure (about 60 atm), in the presence of a phosphoric acid (H3PO4) catalyst.
PART (B)(II) · 3 MARKS
M1
n(C6H12O6) = 3600 / 180 = 20 mol
M2
theoretical n(C2H5OH) = 2 x 20 = 40 mol; theoretical mass = 40 x 46 = 1840 g
A1
% yield = (1500 / 1840) x 100% = 81.5%
PART (B)(III) · 2 MARKS
B1
Ethene is obtained from crude oil/petroleum (fossil fuels), which is a finite resource that cannot be replenished, so it is non-renewable.
B2
Glucose is obtained from crops/plants, which have a relatively short life cycle and can be regrown, so it is a renewable resource.
PART (C)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Propanoic acid
PART (C)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
CH3CH2COOCH2CH3 (ethyl propanoate) — ester linkage -C(=O)-O- between the propanoyl and ethyl groups

questions.question:
A company manufactures polymers and sells one under the trade name 'PB-1'. The table shows information about PB-1: its structure (a drawn repeat unit, not captured as text), molecular mass 5600, and softening temperature 115 C ('softening temperature' is used for materials with no definite melting point).
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
Draw the structural formula of the monomer used to make PB-1.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
Name this monomer.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
What type of polymerisation occurs when PB-1 forms from its monomers?
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
Calculate the number of monomer units in each molecule of low molecular mass PB-1 (Mr = 5600).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
High molecular mass PB-1 has different properties. Suggest the softening temperature of high molecular mass PB-1 and explain your answer.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(III) · 1 MARK
Explain why PB-1 has no definite melting point.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
CH2=CH-CH2-CH3 (but-1-ene)
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
But-1-ene (butene)
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
Addition polymerisation
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
A1
Mr(monomer) = 56; number of monomer units = 5600 / 56 = 100
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
e.g. 130 C (any specific value above 115 C, up to about 500 C)
B2
With a higher molecular mass, the intermolecular forces between chains are stronger and more energy is needed to overcome them, hence a higher softening temperature
PART (B)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
PB-1 is a mixture of macromolecules of different chain lengths (Mr), so there is no single sharp melting point
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
The table shows information about the homologous series of acyl chlorides: ethanoyl chloride CH3COCl, [missing member between ethanoyl and butanoyl chloride], butanoyl chloride C3H7COCl. Ethanoyl chloride reacts with methanol: CH3COCl + CH3OH -> CH3COOCH3 + HCl (compound X).
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
Fill in the table to show the name and displayed formula of the acyl chloride that occurs between ethanoyl chloride and butanoyl chloride in the homologous series.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
Explain how you can tell that these molecules are from the same homologous series.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
Predict the condensed formula of the acyl chloride that contains 7 carbon atoms.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
What is the name of compound X (CH3COOCH3, the product of CH3COCl + CH3OH)?
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
When 64 g of methanol was reacted with excess ethanoyl chloride, 140 g of compound X was obtained. Calculate the percentage yield of compound X.

Draw it
PART (B)(III) · 1 MARK
Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoic acid and methanol.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(IV) · 2 MARKS
Give one similarity and one difference between the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with methanol and the reaction of ethanoic acid with methanol.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Propanoyl chloride, CH3CH2COCl (C2H5COCl)
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
They all contain the same -COCl (acyl chloride) functional group.
B2
Successive members differ by a CH2 unit / they share the same general formula CnH2n+1COCl.
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
C6H13COCl
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Methyl ethanoate
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
M1
n(CH3OH) = 64/32 = 2 mol; theoretical mass of X = 2 x 74 = 148 g
A1
(140/148) x 100% = 94.6%
PART (B)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
CH3COOH + CH3OH <=> CH3COOCH3 + H2O
PART (B)(IV) · 2 MARKS
B1
Both reactions produce the same ester, methyl ethanoate (both are condensation reactions).
B2
The by-product is H2O for ethanoic acid + methanol, but HCl for ethanoyl chloride + methanol.

questions.question:
Fig. 12.1 shows a reaction scheme starting from ethene: ethene + H2 (high temperature, nickel catalyst) -> W; ethene + complete combustion -> Z (+ water); X (glucose) is fermented by yeast at 37 degC in the absence of oxygen to give ethanol; ethanol on standing in air is oxidised to ethanoic acid; ethanoic acid + propanol, heated with a few drops of concentrated H2SO4 (esterification) -> Y (+ water).
Fumaric acid (Fig. 12.2) is a white crystalline compound that dissolves in water to give a colourless solution.
Fumaric acid can undergo condensation polymerisation with ethane-1,2-diol (Fig. 12.3) to form polymer M, and addition polymerisation (via its C=C bond) to form polymer N.
PART (A) · 4 MARKS
Identify W, X, Y and Z in the reaction scheme (Fig. 12.1).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 2 MARKS
Describe what you would observe when aqueous fumaric acid is added to bromine solution, and draw the full structural formula of the product formed.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 1 MARK
Fumaric acid can undergo condensation polymerisation with ethane-1,2-diol to form polymer M. Name the linkage present in M.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(I) · 1 MARK
Draw the structure of polymer N (from addition polymerisation of fumaric acid), showing two repeating units.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(II) · 1 MARK
Define non-biodegradable.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(III) · 1 MARK
Suggest a possible problem that polymer N can pose to our environment during disposal.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 4 MARKS
B1
W = ethane (C2H6)
B2
X = glucose (C6H12O6)
B3
Y = propyl ethanoate (CH3COOC3H7)
B4
Z = carbon dioxide (CO2)
PART (B)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
The reddish-brown (orange) bromine solution turns colourless / is decolourised.
B2
HOOC-CHBr-CHBr-COOH
PART (B)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
Ester linkage
PART (C)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
-[-CH(COOH)-CH(COOH)-]2- : two repeat units, single C-C bonds throughout, COOH group on every backbone carbon.
PART (C)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
A substance that cannot be broken down (decomposed) by bacteria/microorganisms or other natural biological processes into simpler, harmless substances.
PART (C)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
Land pollution: since plastic does not decompose, burying it in landfills causes an increasing build-up of waste over time.
B2
Water pollution: plastic disposed of into the sea can harm/kill marine animals (e.g. through ingestion or entanglement).
B3
Air pollution: plastics are flammable, so incinerating them produces toxic air pollutants; the CO2 released also contributes to global warming (greenhouse effect).

questions.question:
Haloalkanes (CFCs, HFCs, HCFCs, PFCs) are named using prefixes for elements present (PFC = C,F; CFC = C,F,Cl; HFC = H,C,F; HCFC = H,C,F,Cl) and a number suffix: add 90 to the suffix number to get a 3-digit code where the digits give the number of C, H, and F atoms respectively (Cl atoms fill the remaining bonds, since the compounds are saturated).
Letter suffixes (a, b, ...) after the number denote structural isomers ranked by how evenly atomic mass is distributed between the two carbons (no letter = most even; 'a' = second most even; 'b' = third most even).
Example: CFC-113a decodes to 203 -> 2 C, 0 H, 3 F, remaining bonds Cl.
Difluoromethane, CH2F2, an HFC, can be produced from methane via a photochemical free-radical substitution reaction with fluorine.
PART (A) · 1 MARK
Draw the structural formula of a PFC molecule with two carbon atoms.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 1 MARK
A student comments that HFCs are safe alternatives to CFCs as HFCs do not harm the environment like CFCs do. Explain why the student is correct.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 1 MARK
How many fluorine atoms are there in HCFC-132b?
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D) · 2 MARKS
Draw the full structural formulae of HCFC-141a and HCFC-141b.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E)(I) · 1 MARK
Give the condition of the reaction converting methane to difluoromethane, CH2F2.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E)(II) · 2 MARKS
Write equations to show how difluoromethane is produced from methane (with fluorine).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E)(III) · 2 MARKS
Gaseous bromine will also react with methane. Suggest whether the reaction is faster or slower than with fluorine. Explain your reasoning.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
CF3-CF3 (C2F6, hexafluoroethane)
PART (B) · 1 MARK
B1
HFCs do not contain chlorine atoms, which (in CFCs) deplete/damage the ozone layer.
PART (C) · 1 MARK
B1
2 fluorine atoms
PART (D) · 2 MARKS
B1
HCFC-141a: CH2Cl-CHFCl
B2
HCFC-141b: CH3-CFCl2
PART (E)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
UV light
PART (E)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
CH4 + F2 -> CH3F + HF
B2
CH3F + F2 -> CH2F2 + HF
PART (E)(III) · 2 MARKS
B1
Fluorine has a smaller atomic radius than bromine (its valence electrons are closer to the nucleus).
B2
The electrostatic force of attraction between the nucleus and valence electrons is stronger in fluorine.
B3
Fluorine gains electrons more easily / is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.
B4
Fluorine reacts more vigorously than bromine, so the reaction of methane with bromine is slower.
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
1,2-dichloropentanol can be synthesised from pent-1-ene using suitable reagents and conditions. Drawn structures given: 1,2-dichloropentanol — best-effort condensed formula from the diagram is Cl-CH2-CHCl-CH2-CH2-CH2-OH (a pentanol chain bearing two Cl substituents and a terminal OH); pent-1-ene — CH2=CH-CH2-CH2-CH3.
PART (A) · 1 MARK
Draw the full structural formula of an isomer of 1,2-dichloropentanol that can be oxidised to a carboxylic acid.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
1,2-dichloropentanol can be synthesised from pent-1-ene in two separate steps. State the reagents and conditions for each of the reactions involved.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
The labels on the bottles containing pent-1-ene and 1,2-dichloropentanol had dropped off. Describe a chemical test, with expected observations, to identify the compound in each bottle.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
Cl2CH-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-OH (equivalently CHCl2CH2CH2CH2CH2OH) — both Cl atoms moved to the carbon furthest from a terminal -OH.
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
Steam, phosphoric(V) acid (H3PO4) catalyst, high temperature and high pressure — addition/hydration of pent-1-ene to give pentan-1-ol.
B2
Chlorine gas (Cl2), ultraviolet (UV) light — free-radical substitution of two H atoms by two Cl atoms.
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
B1
Add aqueous bromine (bromine water) to a sample from each bottle. (Or: add warm acidified potassium manganate(VII).)
B2
Pent-1-ene decolourises the reddish-brown bromine water (rapidly, with no other condition needed) because of its C=C double bond. (Or: with warm acidified KMnO4, pent-1-ene shows no visible change.)
B3
1,2-dichloropentanol shows no visible change with bromine water (it has no C=C double bond). (Or: with warm acidified KMnO4, 1,2-dichloropentanol decolourises the purple colour.)
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
A table of alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) gives: hydroxyethanoic acid (C2H4O3, pH 1.91 at 1.0 mol/dm3), hydroxypropanoic acid (C3H6O3, pH 1.93), hydroxybutanoic acid (C4H8O3, pH 1.99), hydroxypentanoic acid (C5H10O3, pH 2.07) — pH decreasing (acid strength increasing) as chain length decreases.
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
Describe what is observed when a magnesium strip is placed in a test tube containing hydroxyethanoic acid dissolved in methylbenzene, an organic solvent. Explain your answer.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
Explain how the electrical conductivity of the acid is related to its pH value.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
Excess aqueous sodium carbonate is added to 20.0 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 hydroxyethanoic acid, and the experiment is repeated with the same volume/concentration of hydroxypentanoic acid. Using collision theory, describe and explain the difference in observation between the two experiments.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(I) · 1 MARK
PLA (poly(lactic acid)) can be recycled by depolymerisation. Draw the structure of the product formed.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(II) · 1 MARK
Users of non-biodegradable polymers are encouraged to recycle them. Suggest one economic issue of recycling these polymers.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(III) · 1 MARK
State another chemical method to recycle polymers.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
B1
No visible change / no reaction is observed.
B2
Hydroxyethanoic acid does not ionise in methylbenzene, a non-aqueous organic solvent, so no H+ ions are produced/available to react with the magnesium.
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
A lower pH indicates a stronger acid, which ionises to a greater extent, producing more H+ ions.
B2
More (mobile) ions in solution carry more charge, so electrical conductivity is higher when pH is lower.
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
B1
Hydroxypentanoic acid effervesces/bubbles more slowly than hydroxyethanoic acid (lower rate of gas evolution).
B2
Hydroxypentanoic acid is a weaker acid (lower degree of ionisation), so it has a lower concentration of H+ ions than hydroxyethanoic acid at the same concentration.
B3
With fewer H+ ions present, the frequency of effective collisions between H+ and carbonate ions per unit time is lower, so the rate of reaction is slower.
PART (D)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
CH3-CH(OH)-COOH (lactic acid / 2-hydroxypropanoic acid), the monomer of PLA.
PART (D)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
Recycling can be more expensive than landfill/incineration disposal because of the costs of collecting, transporting, sorting/cleaning and processing the waste plastic.
PART (D)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
Cracking (breaking down the polymer into smaller/useful molecules).
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
Petrol is a mixture of hydrocarbons that includes octane, C8H18.
Exhaust gases from petrol engines contain oxides of carbon and nitrogen which are harmful to the environment.
Thiophene, C4H4S, present in crude oil fractions, produces sulfur dioxide on combustion; combustion of fuels also produces nitrogen dioxide.
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
Write an equation for the complete combustion of octane.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
Suggest a reason why the fuel in an internal combustion engine is unlikely to undergo complete combustion.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
Write an equation to show the removal of carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide from the exhaust gases.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
Explain the effects of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide being released into the atmosphere.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 1 MARK
Explain, in terms of specific processes, how the carbon cycle regulates the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
2C8H18 + 25O2 -> 16CO2 + 18H2O
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
There is insufficient oxygen in the internal combustion engine, hence incomplete combustion occurs.
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
2CO + 2NO -> 2CO2 + N2
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
SO2 and NO2 dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain.
B2
Acid rain leaches nutrients from the soil / lowers the pH of lakes and kills aquatic life / corrodes limestone buildings and statues.
PART (C) · 1 MARK
B1
Carbon dioxide released by combustion, decomposition and respiration is removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis.

questions.question:
Fig. 5.1 shows a reaction scheme starting from an alkene compound, X, which is converted via three reactions using different reagents/conditions: (I) concentrated H2SO4 and HCOOH; (II) H2(g), Ni catalyst; (III) H2O(g), H3PO4, high temperature and pressure, to give products Y and Z respectively. Separately, after the fermentation of sugar from sugarcane to produce ethanol, some ethyl ethanoate is found present in the mixture. 1.00 g of a powder contains 0.30 g glucose (C6H12O6), 0.45 g citric acid (C6H8O7) and 0.25 g sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO3); in water, citric acid reacts with NaHCO3: 3NaHCO3(s) + C6H8O7(aq) -> Na3(C6H5O7)(aq) + 3CO2(g) + 3H2O(l).
PART (A)(I) · 2 MARKS
Draw the organic compounds X and Z.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
Reaction II produces compound Y and one other structural isomer. Draw the full structural formula of the isomer.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
Suggest how ethyl ethanoate may be formed in the fermentation mixture (after fermentation of sugar to produce ethanol).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
Describe the reagents and conditions for a chemical test that gives a positive result ONLY with ethanol (distinguishing it from ethanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate), and describe what would be observed.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(I) · 2 MARKS
Determine the limiting reactant when 1.00 g of the powder (0.45 g citric acid C6H8O7, 0.25 g NaHCO3) reacts, given 3NaHCO3(s) + C6H8O7(aq) -> Na3(C6H5O7)(aq) + 3CO2(g) + 3H2O(l).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(II) · 2 MARKS
0.043 dm3 of CO2 is produced from 1.00 g of the powder. Calculate the percentage yield.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
CH2=CH-CH3 (propene, C3H6)
B2
HCOOC3H7 (propyl methanoate), C4H8O2
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
CH3-CH2-CH2-OH (propan-1-ol) or CH3-CH(OH)-CH3 (propan-2-ol) — whichever differs from Y
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
Ethanol is oxidised by oxygen in the air to form ethanoic acid.
B2
The ethanoic acid formed then reacts with ethanol present in the mixture to form ethyl ethanoate.
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
B1
Heat with acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO4(aq).
B2
Purple KMnO4 solution is decolourised (turns colourless) with ethanol; no change occurs with ethanoic acid or ethyl ethanoate.
PART (D)(I) · 2 MARKS
M1
n(NaHCO3) = 0.25/84 = 0.00298 mol; n(citric acid) = 0.45/192 = 0.00234 mol
A1
NaHCO3 required = 3 x 0.00234 = 0.00703 mol > 0.00298 mol NaHCO3 available, so NaHCO3 is the limiting reactant.
PART (D)(II) · 2 MARKS
M1
Using NaHCO3 (limiting, per d_i): n(CO2) = n(NaHCO3) = 0.00298 mol; V(CO2) = 0.00298 x 24 = 0.0714 dm3. [ECF: if citric acid was named limiting in (d_i): n(CO2) = 3 x 0.00234 = 0.00703 mol; V(CO2) = 0.00703 x 24 = 0.169 dm3]
A1
% yield = (0.043/0.0714) x 100 = 60.2%
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
Electronegativity determines bond polarity: equal electronegativity gives non-polar covalent bonds (Fig 8.1); a difference greater than 0.5 gives a polar covalent bond such as H-Cl (Fig 8.2). Table 8.3 gives electronegativities: H 2.20, C 2.55, N 3.04, O 3.44, Na 0.93, F 3.98, Cl 3.16, Br 2.96. A carboxylic acid dissociates: RCOOH -> RCOO- + H+; the negative charge on RCOO- is delocalised between the two O atoms (resonance). Electron-donating R groups strengthen the negative charge (favouring reformation of RCOOH, weaker acid); electron-withdrawing R groups (with electronegative atoms) weaken it (stronger acid). Table 8.4 gives dissociation constants: -CH3 (ethanoic acid) 1.75x10^-5, -CH2CH3 (propanoic acid) 1.34x10^-5, -CH2Cl (chloroethanoic acid) 1.40x10^-3, -CHCl2 (dichloroethanoic acid) 4.50x10^-2, -CH2Br (bromoethanoic acid) 1.30x10^-3, -CH2F (fluoroethanoic acid) 2.60x10^-3.

PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
Silicon(IV) oxide is a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure with no free ions or delocalised electrons, so there are no charge carriers and it cannot conduct electricity as a solid.
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
Both glass and diamond have a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure.
B2
Both have atoms arranged in a rigid tetrahedral arrangement.

Fig. 6.1 (silica) contains only covalent bonds, whereas Fig. 6.2 glass contains both covalent and ionic bonds.

Fig. 6.1 (silica) contains no ions, whereas Fig. 6.2 glass contains calcium ions and sodium ions.

When the glass is melted, the strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the ions are overcome.

The ions become free to move and act as mobile charge carriers, allowing the molten glass to conduct electricity.

questions.question:
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) have been used as solvents and aerosol propellants.
One widely used CFC is CCl3F.
When CFCs are released into the atmosphere, the C-Cl bond is broken by UV light in a photochemical reaction, releasing chlorine atoms, which break down ozone in a two-step process: step 1: Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2; step 2: ClO + O3 -> Cl + 2O2.
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
By means of a 'dot and cross' diagram, show the arrangement of the electrons in a CCl3F molecule. Show only the valence electrons.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
Explain, in terms of bonding and structure, whether CCl3F would have a high or low boiling point.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(I) · 1 MARK
State the term that is used to describe ozone and oxygen gas.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(II) · 2 MARKS
Use the equations above to explain why the presence of one chlorine molecule in the ozone layer will cause a chain reaction.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(III) · 1 MARK
State the harmful effect that a depleting ozone layer would have on us.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
B1
C shares one electron pair with each of the 3 Cl atoms and the F atom, forming 4 single covalent bonds (dot-and-cross bonding pairs between C and each Cl/F)
B2
Each Cl and the F atom is shown with 3 lone pairs of electrons in addition to the shared bonding pair, so every atom has a complete octet of 8 electrons
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
CCl3F is a simple molecular structure; the molecules are held together by weak intermolecular forces of attraction (van der Waals forces)
B2
Only a small/low amount of energy is needed to overcome these weak intermolecular forces, so CCl3F has a low boiling point
PART (C)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Allotropes
PART (C)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
The ClO formed in step 1 reacts with another O3 molecule in step 2, regenerating (reforming) a Cl atom
B2
This regenerated Cl atom can then repeat/re-enter step 1 and react with more ozone molecules, so one Cl atom destroys many O3 molecules in a repeating (chain) cycle
PART (C)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
More/excessive UV radiation is not absorbed and reaches the Earth's surface, increasing the risk of skin cancer

questions.question:
Calcium nitrate, Ca(NO3)2, and ammonium nitrate, NH4NO3, are ionic compounds used to make fertilisers.
Fig 9.1 shows a simple 2D diagram of how single-charge spherical ions are arranged in a solid ionic compound.
Fig 9.2 outlines the 'bond breaking' (energy absorbed to overcome electrostatic forces between ions) and 'bond forming' (energy released in ion-water interactions) processes when a solid ionic compound dissolves in water.
Fig 9.3 shows the overall energy changes when solid calcium nitrate and solid ammonium nitrate each dissolve in water.
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
Give two reasons why Fig 9.1 is a better representation for the ions in solid ammonium nitrate than the ions in solid calcium nitrate.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 1 MARK
Suggest one other reason (besides ion size) why Fig 9.1 does not accurately represent a solid ionic compound.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 4 MARKS
Using Fig 9.2 and Fig 9.3, describe and explain the differences in the overall energy changes when calcium nitrate and ammonium nitrate dissolve in water.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(I) · 2 MARKS
Describe the steps required to prepare a solution of calcium nitrate, starting with powdered calcium carbonate.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(II) · 1 MARK
Ammonium nitrate can be prepared by the method of titration. Suggest a suitable pair of reagents that react to produce ammonium nitrate.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
B1
NH4+ and NO3- ions each carry a single charge (1+ and 1- respectively), matching the single-charge spheres shown in Fig 9.1.
B2
The calcium ion, Ca2+, carries a 2+ charge, which the single-charge spheres in Fig 9.1 do not show.
B3
There is a 1:1 ratio of NH4+ to NO3- ions in ammonium nitrate, matching the equal numbers of ions shown in Fig 9.1.
B4
There is a 1:2 ratio of Ca2+ to NO3- ions in calcium nitrate, which is not shown by the equal (1:1) numbers of ions in Fig 9.1.
PART (B) · 1 MARK
B1
NO3- (and NH4+) are polyatomic ions made up of several atoms, so they cannot be accurately shown as a single sphere.
B2
Real ions are not perfectly spherical, unlike the spheres drawn in Fig 9.1.
B3
The ions vibrate about fixed positions in the solid, which Fig 9.1 does not show.
B4
A real ionic solid contains a huge number of ions, with the lattice extending much further than the few ions shown in Fig 9.1.
B5
Fig 9.1 is only a 2D diagram, but the ions in a real ionic lattice are arranged in three dimensions.
PART (C) · 4 MARKS
B1
The overall energy change is greater in magnitude for calcium nitrate than for ammonium nitrate.
B2
Delta H is negative (exothermic) for calcium nitrate, but delta H is positive (endothermic) for ammonium nitrate.
B3
For calcium nitrate, more (heat) energy is released during bond forming than is absorbed during bond breaking, giving a net exothermic change; for ammonium nitrate, more (heat) energy is absorbed during bond breaking than is released during bond forming, giving a net endothermic change.
B4
The gap between the energy absorbed in bond breaking and the energy released in bond forming is much bigger for calcium nitrate than for ammonium nitrate, which is why its overall energy change has the bigger magnitude.
PART (D)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
Add (excess) powdered calcium carbonate to nitric acid.
B2
Stir until no more bubbles/effervescence are produced, then filter to remove excess calcium carbonate and collect the filtrate (calcium nitrate solution).
PART (D)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
Aqueous ammonia (or ammonium carbonate) and (dilute) nitric acid.

Draw it

Draw it

Two students make statements about %H by mass in the hydrides: Student 1 says more H atoms means greater %H by mass; Student 2 says %H by mass is the same for hydrides with the same number of H atoms. Does Table 5.1 support each statement? Explain.

Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
NaH + H2O -> NaOH + H2
PART (B) · 1 MARK
B1
If the pH of the resulting solution is more than 10 (strongly alkaline), the hydride is a metal hydride. If the pH is 10 or below (only slightly alkaline, neutral, or acidic), the hydride is a non-metal hydride.
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
B1
Na+ ion, with no electrons shown in its outer shell (it has lost its one outer/valence electron).
B2
[H]- ion in square brackets, showing 2 outer electrons (1 dot from H's own electron, 1 cross transferred from Na), with an overall single negative charge.
PART (D) · 2 MARKS
B1
In the solid, the ions are held in fixed positions in the giant ionic lattice, so there are no free-moving ions to carry charge/conduct electricity.
B2
When molten, the giant ionic lattice breaks down and the ions are free to move, so they can carry charge and conduct electricity.

B1
Student 1 is correct: SiH4 has 4 H atoms, the most of any hydride in the table, and %H = 4/32 x 100% = 12.5%, the highest value, supporting the statement.

Student 2 is wrong: PH3 and AlH3 both have 3 H atoms, but %H in PH3 = 3/34 x 100% = 8.8% while %H in AlH3 = 3/30 x 100% = 10%, which are different, disproving the statement.

Adding a small volume of aqueous NaOH to Cu2+ ions gives a light-blue precipitate of Cu(H2O)4(OH)2 (unchanged in excess NaOH).
Adding a small volume of aqueous ammonia to Cu2+ ions also gives Cu(H2O)4(OH)2; when aqueous ammonia is added in excess, four ammonia ligands replace the two OH- ligands and two H2O ligands.

Draw the dot-and-cross diagram of ammonium chloride, showing only the outer shell electrons.

Suggest the molecular formula of the complex ion of iron(II) after adding excess aqueous ammonia.

With reference to the complex ions of both metals, explain the difference in observations when excess aqueous ammonia is added to copper(II) and iron(II) solutions in separate test tubes.

questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
NH4+: nitrogen forms three ordinary covalent bonds (one electron each from N and H) to three H atoms, and a fourth coordinate (dative) bond to the fourth H+ in which both electrons come from nitrogen's lone pair; N ends with a complete octet of 8 electrons, each H has a duet of 2.

B1
A light blue precipitate of Cu(H2O)4(OH)2 forms.
B2
The light blue precipitate dissolves in excess NH3(aq), forming a dark blue solution of [Cu(H2O)2(NH3)4]2+.

B1
[Cu(H2O)2(NH3)4]2+
PART (B)(III) · 2 MARKS
B1
2 H2O and 4 NH3 ligands arranged around Cu2+, each bonded via a coordinate-bond arrow pointing from the ligand's donor atom toward the central Cu.
B2
[Cu(H2O)2(NH3)4]2+ — the full ion enclosed in square brackets with a 2+ charge shown outside.
PART (C)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Fe(H2O)4(OH)2 — unchanged from the precipitate formed with a small volume of ammonia, since iron(II) hydroxide does not undergo ligand exchange with excess ammonia.

B1
Cu(H2O)4(OH)2 undergoes ligand exchange with excess NH3 to form soluble [Cu(H2O)2(NH3)4]2+, but Fe(H2O)4(OH)2 remains insoluble in excess aqueous ammonia (no ligand exchange occurs for iron).

On standing, the surface of the green precipitate is exposed to oxygen in the air.

Green Fe(OH)2 is oxidised (by the oxygen in air) to red-brown Fe(OH)3, which is the red-brown surface layer.

questions.question:
Diamond and silicon carbide have giant molecular structures; part of the structure of silicon carbide is shown. Silicon tetrachloride, SiCl4, is another compound of silicon: a colourless, volatile liquid with melting point -68.7C and boiling point 57.6C.
PART (A)(I) · 2 MARKS
State one similarity and one difference in structure between silicon carbide and diamond.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 4 MARKS
Silicon carbide is hard and is a poor conductor of electricity. Explain why in terms of bonding.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
Suggest one possible use of silicon carbide.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
State the structure of silicon tetrachloride, SiCl4.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
Explain, in terms of the bonding present, why the melting point of silicon tetrachloride is low.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
Similarity: both are giant structures in which each atom is bonded tetrahedrally to four other atoms (each Si to 4 C in SiC, each C to 4 C in diamond).
B2
Difference: silicon carbide contains two elements (silicon and carbon) bonded together, whereas diamond consists of only one element, carbon.
PART (A)(II) · 4 MARKS
B1
Each silicon atom is bonded to four carbon atoms (and each carbon atom to four silicon atoms) by strong covalent bonds throughout a giant 3-D structure.
B2
A lot of (heat) energy is needed to break the many strong covalent bonds in the giant structure, making silicon carbide hard.
B3
All four valence electrons of each silicon and carbon atom are used up in (localised) covalent bonding.
B4
There are no mobile/delocalised electrons (or ions) in the structure, so silicon carbide cannot conduct electricity.
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
Used in drills / cutting tools (accept other uses reflecting its hardness, e.g. abrasives or grinding wheels).
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Simple molecular (simple covalent) structure.
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
There are (only) weak intermolecular forces of attraction (van der Waals forces) between silicon tetrachloride molecules.
B2
Little (heat) energy is required to overcome these weak intermolecular forces; the strong covalent bonds within each molecule are not broken on melting.

questions.question:
Carbon is a highly versatile element that exists in different forms such as diamond, graphite and fullerene.
Figure 7.1 shows the structure of graphite: flat layers of carbon atoms, each carbon atom joined to only three other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds within a layer, with weak forces holding the layers together.
Figure 7.2 shows the structure of a buckyball, C60 -- a cage-like fullerene of 60 carbon atoms covalently bonded, made of twenty hexagons and twelve pentagons, resembling a soccer ball.
PART (A) · 1 MARK
State a physical property of graphite.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
By comparing the structures of graphite and buckyball, predict if buckyball can conduct electricity. Explain your answer.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
Graphite has a high melting point (strong covalent bonds within each layer require a lot of energy to break).
B2
Graphite is insoluble in water (though it may dissolve in certain organic solvents).
B3
Graphite conducts electricity (due to delocalised electrons that are free to move within each layer).
B4
Graphite is soft and slippery/brittle, because the weak forces between layers let the layers slide over one another.
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
Like graphite, each carbon atom in buckyball is covalently bonded to only 3 other carbon atoms, so there is 1 delocalised (unbonded) electron per carbon atom, free to move and carry charge.
B2
Buckyball can conduct electricity.

PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
Strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions (positive and negative ions / cations and anions) throughout the lattice

B1
A (regular) lattice of positive metal ions (cations)
B2
surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalised (mobile) electrons

Giant covalent structures contain only atoms; there are no ions present

When molten (liquid), the ions are free to move and can carry charge, so molten ionic compounds are good conductors
B5
Metals have delocalised (mobile) electrons in both the solid and liquid states, so metals are good conductors whether solid or molten

questions.question:
Practical: investigate the enthalpy change when solid Na2CO3 reacts with excess dilute HCl(aq).
Equation: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + CO2 + H2O.
Method: weigh container with Na2CO3; add 100 cm3 HCl(aq) (excess) to a Styrofoam cup; record temperature every minute for 0-2 min; at 3 min transfer the Na2CO3 solid into the cup and stir; continue recording temperature every minute up to 8 min; reweigh the container with any residual solid.
Plot temperature against time, draw two best-fit lines (0-2 min and 4-8 min) extrapolated to 3 min and joined by a vertical line at 3 min, to find the maximum temperature change. heat change (J) = mass of solution (g) x maximum temperature change (C) x 4.2, assuming 1.0 cm3 of solution has mass 1.0 g. [Mr: Na2CO3, 106].
Also: identify a source of error and an improvement; and describe a test (with expected observations) for barium carbonate contamination in the sodium carbonate sample.
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
The maximum temperature change was determined from the temperature-time graph to be 3.6 deg C. Given that 100 cm3 of the HCl(aq) was used (1.0 cm3 of solution is assumed to have a mass of 1.0 g), use the expression heat change (J) = mass of solution (g) x maximum temperature change (deg C) x 4.2 to calculate the heat change for this reaction, in J.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(IV) · 1 MARK
5.12 g of Na2CO3 was used in the experiment (Mr of Na2CO3 = 106). Calculate the number of moles of Na2CO3 used.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(V) · 2 MARKS
Using your answers to (a)(iii) and (a)(iv), calculate the enthalpy change of reaction, in kJ/mol, for one mole of sodium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid. Include the appropriate sign to show whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and give the numerical answers to (a)(iii), (a)(iv) and (a)(v) all to 3 significant figures.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(VI) · 3 MARKS
State one source of error in the experimental results, explain its effect on the value of the enthalpy change of reaction calculated, and suggest one improvement that could be made to reduce this error.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
Describe briefly how you would test a sample of the solid sodium carbonate for the presence of barium carbonate, including the expected observation(s).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
M1
heat change = 100 x 3.6 x 4.2 = 1512 J (= 1510 J to 3 s.f.)
PART (A)(IV) · 1 MARK
M1
moles of Na2CO3 = 5.12/106 = 0.0483 mol (3 s.f.)
PART (A)(V) · 2 MARKS
A1
enthalpy change = -(1512/0.0483) = -31300 J/mol = -31.3 kJ/mol
B1
1510 J (3 s.f.); 0.0483 mol (3 s.f.); -31.3 kJ/mol (3 s.f.)
PART (A)(VI) · 3 MARKS
B1
heat loss to the surroundings during the reaction
B2
because heat is lost to the surroundings (or as spray) instead of heating the solution, the maximum temperature change recorded -- and hence the magnitude of the enthalpy change of reaction calculated -- will be smaller than the true value
B3
cover the Styrofoam cup with a (plastic) lid, with a hole for the thermometer, immediately after adding the sodium carbonate

B1
add (excess) dilute sulfuric acid, H2SO4(aq), to a sample of the sodium carbonate
B2
a white precipitate (of barium sulfate, BaSO4) forms if BaCO3 is present; no precipitate forms if BaCO3 is absent

B1

Energy released in forming N-H bonds (2346 kJ) is greater than energy absorbed in breaking H-H and N#N bonds (2253 kJ), so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.question:
Sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs) are made by processing used cooking oil (removing impurities such as water) and blending the processed oil with jet fuel obtained from crude oil (Fig. 3.1 flow chart: crude oil -> jet fuel + other fractions; used cooking oil -> impurities + processed oil; jet fuel + processed oil + other -> SAFs).
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
Name the separation process to obtain jet fuel from crude oil.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
Explain how this process separates crude oil into fractions including jet fuel.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
Describe how a separating funnel can be used to separate processed oil from impurities (water) in used cooking oil.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
Discuss the carbon cycle and explain why burning bioethanol (from sugarcane) might not always be considered carbon neutral.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D) · 2 MARKS
Using bond energies (C-C 350, C=C 610, C-O 358, O=O 496, C-H 410, C=O 799, O-H 460 kJ/mol), calculate the enthalpy change for C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E) · 3 MARKS
Complete the energy profile diagram for the combustion of ethanol, including reactant/product formulae, the enthalpy change, and the activation energy.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Fractional distillation.
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
Crude oil is heated in a furnace to form a vapour, which enters the fractionating column. As the vapour rises, fractions with lower boiling points rise further up the column and condense there, while fractions with higher boiling points condense lower down the column.
B2
Jet fuel is collected as one of the fractions, at the level of the column corresponding to its boiling point.
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
The used cooking oil (containing water) is placed in the separating funnel and allowed to settle; the oil and water are immiscible and separate into two layers due to their different densities.
B2
The tap is opened to run off the denser water layer (at the bottom) first; the tap is closed once the water has drained, leaving the processed oil behind in the funnel.
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
B1
Burning bioethanol releases CO2 into the atmosphere, while the sugarcane plants (from which the bioethanol is made) had earlier absorbed CO2 during photosynthesis as they grew.
B2
This means there is no net increase in atmospheric CO2 — the process is considered carbon neutral, as the CO2 released is offset by the CO2 absorbed by the sugarcane during photosynthesis.
B3
However, other processes such as clearing land for sugarcane plantations and burning fossil fuels to farm and transport the sugarcane/bioethanol release additional CO2, so the process is not always fully carbon neutral.
PART (D) · 2 MARKS
M1
Energy to break bonds in reactants = 350 + 5(410) + 358 + 460 + 3(496) = 4706 kJ; energy released forming bonds in products = 4(799) + 6(460) = 5956 kJ.
A1
ΔH = energy absorbed - energy released = 4706 - 5956 = -1250 kJ.
PART (E) · 3 MARKS
B1

B2
Ea is labelled as the energy difference from the reactants' level up to the peak (the maximum point) of the curve.
B3
ΔH is labelled as the drop in energy from the reactants' level down to the products' level, equal to -1250 kJ (candidate's own (d) value, ECF).

questions.question:

Draw it

Attach photo or sketch

questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
The high temperature in the car engine causes nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react together, forming nitrogen monoxide (nitrogen oxides).
B2
Carbon monoxide is formed by the incomplete combustion of fuel (petrol), owing to an insufficient/limited supply of oxygen in the engine.

Nitrogen monoxide irritates the eyes and lungs, causing breathing difficulties/respiratory problems.

Catalytic converters do not remove carbon dioxide; carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas, so it is still released and continues to cause global warming.

questions.question:

(i)

(ii)

questions.question:
Determine the enthalpy change for the metal displacement reaction Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) → ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s), using 25 cm3 of T (0.800 mol/dm3 copper(II) sulfate) in a Styrofoam cup and excess zinc powder S (~3 g), added at t = 1.5 min. The pre-addition (before zinc is added) straight best-fit line and the cooling (after zinc is added) straight best-fit line on the temperature-time graph are each extrapolated to t = 1.5 min: the pre-addition line reads 30.0°C at t = 1.5 min and the cooling line reads 67.5°C at t = 1.5 min. Use a lid on the Styrofoam cup to reduce heat loss to the surroundings.

energy density = |enthalpy of combustion| / Mr = 5133 / 128 = 40.1 kJ/g
PART (B) · 1 MARK
B1
Naphthalene is better because it has a higher energy density (40.1 kJ/g vs 30 kJ/g), so less mass of it is needed to give out the same amount of energy, which is an advantage for camping where fuel must be carried
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
B1
Nitrogen dioxide (NO2)
B2
NO2 dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, which corrodes limestone/metal structures and harms aquatic plants and animals
PART (D)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
Student A: the white solid dissolves in the acid. Student B: the white solid dissolves in the alkali (or a white precipitate is seen)
B2
Aluminium oxide is amphoteric, so it reacts with both acids and bases (alkalis)
PART (D)(II) · 3 MARKS
B1
Aluminium oxide has a giant ionic lattice structure, held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged Al3+ and O2- ions
B2
Nitrogen dioxide has a simple molecular structure, with only weak intermolecular forces of attraction between molecules
B3
Al2O3's strong ionic bonds need a lot of energy to overcome, so it has a high melting point and is a solid at r.t.p.; NO2's weak intermolecular forces need little energy to overcome, so it has a low melting/boiling point and is a gas at r.t.p.

questions.question:
Metal R is more reactive than iron and displaces iron from aqueous iron(II) sulfate (exothermic reaction). 2.0 g of powdered R is added to boiling tubes each containing a total of 10 cm3 of aqueous iron(II) sulfate (0.500 mol/dm3) diluted with distilled water to different extents (volumes of FeSO4(aq) : distilled water = 10:0, 8:2, 6:4, 4:6, 2:8). Initial and highest temperatures are recorded for each experiment: 1) 30.0->46.5C, 2) 29.5->44.5C, 3) 29.0->41.0C, 4) 29.5->37.0C, 5) 29.5->33.0C.
PART (A) · 1 MARK
Complete the results table by calculating the change in temperature for each of the 5 experiments.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(I) · 2 MARKS
Describe and explain the trend shown by the graph in (b).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(II) · 2 MARKS
Determine the expected change in temperature if the experiment was repeated with 0.0035 mol of iron(II) sulfate in the 10 cm3 of solution, showing clearly on the graph how the answer was obtained.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(III) · 1 MARK
Predict the change in temperature if 2.0 g of metal R was added to 10 cm3 of 1.00 mol/dm3 iron(II) sulfate.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 1 MARK
A1
deltaT = T(highest) - T(initial): 46.5-30.0=16.5; 44.5-29.5=15.0; 41.0-29.0=12.0; 37.0-29.5=7.5; 33.0-29.5=3.5 (degC)
PART (C)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
the larger the volume of iron(II) sulfate solution used, the greater the change in temperature (roughly directly proportional / straight-line relationship)
B2
a greater volume of iron(II) sulfate means more moles of iron(II) sulfate react with R, releasing more heat energy, giving a larger temperature rise
PART (C)(II) · 2 MARKS
M1
volume = n / c = 0.0035 mol / 0.500 mol/dm3 = 0.007 dm3 = 7 cm3
A1
at volume = 7 cm3 on the straight line of best fit, the expected change in temperature is approximately 12.4 degC
PART (C)(III) · 1 MARK
A1
doubling the concentration from 0.500 to 1.00 mol/dm3 (same 10 cm3 volume) doubles the moles of FeSO4 reacting, so the temperature change doubles: 16.5 x 2 = 33.0 degC

questions.question:
The combustion of ethanol or hydrogen releases energy, enabling their use as fuels.
Complete combustion of ethanol: C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O, deltaH = -1370 kJ per mole of C2H5OH.
Complete combustion of hydrogen: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.
Bond energies (kJ/mol): H-H 436, O=O 496, O-H 460.
Hydrogen and ethanol can also be used in fuel cells — a direct ethanol fuel cell (DEFC) has negative-electrode half-equation: C2H5OH + 3H2O -> 2CO2 + 12H+ + 12e-.
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond making, why this reaction is exothermic.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
Use the bond energies given to calculate the energy released on burning 1 mole of hydrogen (2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(I) · 1 MARK
Calculate the energy released when 1 g of hydrogen is burned in excess oxygen.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(II) · 1 MARK
Calculate the energy released when 1 g of ethanol is burned in excess oxygen.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(I) · 1 MARK
With reference to the diagram, what would be the half-equation at the positive electrode in a DEFC?
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(II) · 1 MARK
Write the overall equation for the reaction occurring in a DEFC.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
more energy is released when new bonds form in the products, CO2 and H2O
B2
this is more than the energy absorbed breaking bonds in the reactants, C2H5OH and O2, so there is a net release of energy to the surroundings and the temperature rises
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
M1
energy change = [2(436) + 496] - [4(460)] = 872 + 496 - 1840 = -472 kJ (for 2 mol H2 reacting)
A1
236 kJ per mole of H2 (472 kJ / 2 mol)
PART (C)(I) · 1 MARK
A1
118 kJ (= 236 kJ/mol ÷ 2 g/mol)
PART (C)(II) · 1 MARK
A1
29.8 kJ (= 1370 kJ/mol ÷ 46 g/mol)
PART (D)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O
PART (D)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O

questions.question:
Planning question: when zinc powder is added to aqueous copper(II) sulfate, an exothermic reaction occurs: CuSO4(aq) + Zn(s) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s), delta H < 0.
Plan a procedure to determine a value for delta T max (the maximum temperature change) for this reaction, given aqueous copper(II) sulfate, powdered zinc solid, and standard school laboratory equipment.
The plan should include: apparatus used, procedure followed, measurements made, and how the measurements are used to calculate delta T max.
PART (A) · 4 MARKS
Plan a procedure (apparatus, method, measurements, and calculation) to determine ΔTmax for the reaction between zinc powder and aqueous copper(II) sulfate.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
Describe and explain the expected observations during the reaction between zinc powder and aqueous copper(II) sulfate.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
Jane added 0.5 g of zinc to 100 cm3 of 0.1 mol/dm3 aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Show, by calculation, that zinc is the limiting reagent. [Ar of Zn = 65]
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D) · 1 MARK
Jane found that ΔTmax for her experiment was +6.5°C. Calculate the enthalpy change, ΔH, of the reaction using the given equation: ΔH = -[V x c x ΔTmax] / [moles of limiting reagent], where V is the volume of copper(II) sulfate in cm3 and c = 4.2 (J/g°C).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 4 MARKS
B1
Weigh out a stated mass of Zn powder (e.g. 0.5 g); measure out a stated volume of CuSO4(aq) (e.g. 50.0 cm3) using a measuring cylinder
B2
Use a polystyrene cup nested inside a 250 cm3 beaker (for support/insulation), with a measuring cylinder to measure the CuSO4(aq) and an electronic balance to weigh the Zn powder
B3
Record the initial temperature of the CuSO4(aq), T1; add the Zn powder and stir continuously with the thermometer, recording the highest temperature reached, T2
B4
ΔTmax = T2 - T1
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
The blue colour of the CuSO4(aq) fades (becomes paler/colourless) because the concentration of Cu2+ ions decreases as the reaction proceeds
B2
A reddish-brown solid (copper) is deposited, because Zn is more reactive than Cu and displaces copper from the copper(II) sulfate solution
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
M1
moles Zn = 0.5/65 = 0.00769 mol; moles CuSO4 = (100/1000) x 0.1 = 0.01 mol
B1
Since the mole ratio Zn:CuSO4 is 1:1, 0.01 mol of CuSO4 would require 0.01 mol of Zn, but only 0.00769 mol of Zn is available, so Zn is the limiting reagent
PART (D) · 1 MARK
A1
ΔH = -(100 x 4.2 x 6.5) / 0.00769 = -355 000 J/mol (3 s.f.), ecf from (c)

questions.question:
Practical investigation: the reaction of magnesium and dilute hydrochloric acid is exothermic. Candidates carry out five experiments reacting a fixed amount of magnesium ribbon (2 pieces, 1 cm each) with different volumes of P (1.000 mol/dm3 HCl) made up to 10 cm3 total with water (10+0, 8+2, 6+4, 4+6, 2+8 cm3 of P+water), record initial and highest temperature, and calculate the temperature change for each experiment.
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
Describe and explain the trend shown by the graph in (b): how the temperature change varies with the volume of P used.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
A student repeats the experiment using 10 cm3 of P and four pieces (double) of magnesium ribbon, predicting the temperature change would be twice that of Experiment 1. Explain if his prediction was correct, and state the assumption made in the prediction.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (F) · 4 MARKS
Give two observations, other than temperature change, made when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, and explain each observation.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (G) · 2 MARKS
State one source of error, other than heat loss, in the results obtained in Experiments 1 to 5, and suggest one improvement to reduce this error.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
B1
As the volume of P used increases, the temperature rise (change in temperature) also increases.
B2
A greater volume of P contains a greater number of moles of hydrochloric acid to react with the fixed amount of magnesium, so more heat/energy is released, giving a bigger temperature rise.
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
B1
The prediction is not correct. Although the amount of magnesium is doubled, there may not be enough acid to react completely with all of the magnesium (the acid could be the limiting reagent), so the amount of energy produced, and hence the temperature rise, may not double.
B2
Assumption: there is enough (excess) acid present to react completely with all the magnesium (i.e. the acid is not used up / is not the limiting reagent).
PART (F) · 4 MARKS
B1
Effervescence (bubbles) is seen.
B2
The bubbles/effervescence are due to hydrogen gas being produced.
B3
The magnesium ribbon dissolves/disappears, forming a colourless solution.
B4
Soluble magnesium chloride is formed.
PART (G) · 2 MARKS
B1
A measuring cylinder was used to measure volumes of P and water, which is not very accurate/precise. Improvement: use a burette instead, which can measure volumes more precisely.
B2
A laboratory thermometer was used to measure temperature, which is only accurate to 0.5 degC. Improvement: use a temperature sensor and data logger, which gives more precise readings.
B3
Each experiment was carried out only once, so the results are not reliable. Improvement: repeat each experiment and calculate the average temperature change.
B4
The measuring cylinder was washed with water after each use and still contained residual water, diluting the acid measured out. Improvement: use a dry measuring cylinder for each experiment.
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
[Section B, answer ONE of Q9/Q10] Scientists investigated the chemical behaviour and thermal stability of different carbonates.
Experiment 1: sodium carbonate and magnesium carbonate were each added to separate beakers of equal volume/concentration nitric acid; sodium carbonate reacts faster; pH of sodium carbonate solution was 11 before nitric acid was added and dropped to 3 after excess acid was added.
Experiment 2: magnesium carbonate and copper(II) carbonate were heated separately in test tubes; the gas from MgCO3 decomposition was passed through limewater (initial precipitate, then observed for longer exposure); the decomposition of MgCO3 is endothermic.
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
Write an ionic equation for the reaction between carbonate ions and hydrogen ions.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
Sodium carbonate reacts faster than magnesium carbonate with nitric acid. Explain this observation in terms of solubility and ion availability.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
The pH of sodium carbonate solution was 11 before nitric acid was added, and dropped to 3 after excess nitric acid was added. Explain this change in terms of the ions present and their concentrations.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(IV) · 2 MARKS
Predict and explain the difference in the total volume of gas produced when equal masses of sodium carbonate and magnesium carbonate are used (assuming complete reaction).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
Write an equation for the thermal decomposition of magnesium carbonate.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
The gas from thermal decomposition of magnesium carbonate was passed through limewater; a precipitate formed initially. Identify the precipitate and state what happens when the gas is passed through limewater for a longer time.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(III) · 2 MARKS
The decomposition of magnesium carbonate is endothermic. Explain, in terms of bond breaking and bond forming, why the overall enthalpy change for this reaction is positive.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
2H+(aq) + CO3^2-(aq) -> H2O(l) + CO2(g)
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
Na2CO3 is more soluble than MgCO3, so more CO3^2- ions are available (in solution) to react with the H+ from the acid.
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
Before acid is added: high concentration of OH- ions gives pH 11. After excess acid is added: high concentration of H+ ions (from the excess acid) lowers the pH to 3.
PART (A)(IV) · 2 MARKS
B1
Na2CO3 produces less gas (CO2) than MgCO3 for the same mass used.
B2
Mr(Na2CO3) = 106 > Mr(MgCO3) = 84, so equal mass gives fewer moles of Na2CO3, hence fewer moles of CO2 (1:1 with carbonate) than from MgCO3.
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
MgCO3 -> MgO + CO2
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
The precipitate is calcium carbonate.
B2
With excess CO2, the CaCO3 precipitate dissolves, forming soluble Ca(HCO3)2, so the solution becomes colourless/clear again.
PART (B)(III) · 2 MARKS
B1
Bonds are broken in MgCO3, absorbing energy; bonds are formed in MgO and CO2, releasing energy.
B2
Energy absorbed (bond breaking) > energy released (bond forming), so the overall enthalpy change is positive (endothermic).
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
P is dilute sulfuric acid; Q is 1.23 mol/dm3 aqueous sodium hydroxide. In 7 experiments, varying volumes of P and Q (total 50 cm3 each time: 40+10, 35+15, 30+20, 25+25, 20+30, 15+35, 10+40) are mixed in a Styrofoam cup and the highest temperature reached is recorded. (a) Complete the results table and calculate the temperature rise for each experiment. (b) Plot temperature rise (y) against volume of Q (x) and draw two intersecting straight lines of best fit. (c) Read off the volume of Q and temperature rise at the intersection.

Write the equation for NaOH + H2SO4.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(II) · 1 MARK
Calculate moles of P needed to neutralise the volume of Q found in (c).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(III) · 1 MARK
Calculate the volume of P needed.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(IV) · 2 MARKS
Calculate the concentration of H2SO4 in P.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
Using energy change (J) = mass of solution (g) x max temperature rise (C) x 4.2, and density of solution = 1.05 g/cm3, calculate the energy change to 1 d.p.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (F) · 2 MARKS
Student A says acid R (same concentration, half the max temperature, twice the volume needed) is a strong monobasic acid; Student B says it is a weak dibasic acid. Comment on both statements.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (D)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O
PART (D)(II) · 1 MARK
M1
moles of NaOH = (volume of Q / 1000) x 1.23; moles of H2SO4 = moles of NaOH / 2 (model working using volume of Q = 24.5 cm3: 0.03014 / 2 = 0.0151 mol)
PART (D)(III) · 1 MARK
M1
volume of P = 50 - volume of Q (model working: 50 - 24.5 = 25.5 cm3)
PART (D)(IV) · 2 MARKS
M1
concentration of H2SO4 = moles of H2SO4 (from (d)(ii)) / (volume of P in cm3 (from (d)(iii)) / 1000) [model working: 0.0151 / (25.5/1000) = 0.591 mol/dm3]
B1
Volume of P in cm3; concentration of H2SO4 in mol/dm3.
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
M1
energy change (J) = (50 x 1.05) x temperature rise (from (c)) x 4.2 [model working: 50 x 1.05 x 4.2 x 7.8 = 1719.9 J]
B1
Energy change = -1719.9 J (negative sign shown to indicate exothermic; 1 d.p.)
PART (F) · 2 MARKS
B1
Both a weak acid and a monobasic acid give a lower [H+] and hence a lower maximum temperature rise, so the halved temperature alone does not distinguish between the two explanations.
B2
A weak dibasic acid would need the same volume as H2SO4 to neutralise the alkali (both supply 2 H+ per mole); since twice the volume of R was actually needed, R must be monobasic, supporting Student A and contradicting Student B.
