questions.question:
You are investigating the temperature changes when two solids, C and D, dissolve in water.
Experiment 1: in turn, add 5 g, 7 g and 8 g samples of solid C to 40 cm3 of deionised water in a polystyrene cup (supported in a 250 cm3 beaker), stir with the thermometer and measure the temperature after 1 minute each time; record initial temperature, temperature after 1 min, and temperature change (+ or -).
Experiment 2: repeat using 3 g, 4 g, 6 g and 8 g samples of solid D, recording results in a table of your own construction.
(c)
Plot temperature change against mass of solid added for both solids on the grid provided, including the origin, with two labelled straight best-fit lines.
(d)
-(h) use the results/graph to answer further questions on the enthalpy change, predicted temperatures, effect of using 80 cm3 of water, and how to improve accuracy.
PART (E) · 1 MARK
State whether ΔH, the enthalpy change when solid C dissolves in water, is positive or negative, and explain your answer
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (F) · 1 MARK
Use your experimental data to suggest the temperature of the solution containing 8 g of solid D if the solution were left for 2 hours
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (G) · 2 MARKS
Suggest how the temperature changes measured after 1 minute would differ if the experiments were repeated using 80 cm3 instead of 40 cm3 of deionised water in each case
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (H) · 2 MARKS
Suggest one change you could make to the experiments to obtain more accurate results, and explain how this change would make the results more accurate
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (E) · 1 MARK
B1
Positive. Dissolving of solid C is endothermic — it absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the temperature of the solution falls.
PART (F) · 1 MARK
B1
The temperature will fall back to (approximately) the initial temperature of the deionised water / room temperature, since heat is gradually lost to the surroundings over the 2 hours.
PART (G) · 2 MARKS
B1
The temperature change would be smaller/lower for both solids.
B2
The temperature change would be halved for both solid C and solid D, because the same amount of heat energy released/absorbed is now spread over twice the mass of water.
PART (H) · 2 MARKS
B1
Use a pipette or burette (instead of a measuring cylinder) to measure the 40 cm3 of deionised water.
B2
A pipette/burette measures the volume of water more accurately than a measuring cylinder can. (Or: a lid reduces heat loss/gain to/from the surroundings, so the temperature change measured is more accurate.)

questions.question:
The 'iodine clock' reaction: aqueous potassium iodide is mixed with a fixed volume of starch and iron(III) salt solutions, producing iodine which turns blue-black with starch. Table 6.1 gives 5 experiments varying volume of KI, volume of distilled water, temperature and catalyst, with the time for blue-black colour to appear: Expt1: 3.0cm3 KI,7.0cm3 water,20C,no catalyst,50s; Expt2: 6.0,4.0,20C,no catalyst,27s; Expt3: 6.0,4.0,20C,silver catalyst,26s; Expt4: 6.0,4.0,20C,copper catalyst,20s; Expt5: 6.0,4.0,40C,no catalyst,15s.
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
Explain how a catalyst affects reaction rates.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
Using Table 6.1, compare the effectiveness of copper and silver as catalysts.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 4 MARKS
Using ideas about particle collisions and Table 6.1 values, explain why changing concentration and temperature affects the time taken for the blue-black colour to appear.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
Explain the importance of starch in the experiments.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so the reaction proceeds faster / the rate of reaction increases.
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
With copper, the time drops from 27 s (Expt 2, no catalyst) to 20 s (Expt 4) — a decrease of 7 s. With silver, the time only drops from 27 s to 26 s (Expt 3) — a decrease of just 1 s.
B2
Copper is an effective catalyst for this reaction, but silver is not an effective catalyst (its effect on the rate is negligible).

B1
Comparing Expt 1 and Expt 4: [S2O8^2-] is unchanged but [I-] doubles (0.02 -> 0.04 mol/dm3) and the rate doubles (1.7 -> 3.4), so rate is directly proportional to [I-]. 0.00016 mol S2O8^2- requires 2 x 0.00016 = 0.00032 mol I- (1:2 ratio). Since the I- present (0.0004 mol in Expt 4, 0.0008 mol in Expt 5) exceeds 0.00032 mol in both cases, I- is in excess in both experiments, so S2O8^2- is the limiting reactant in both experiment 4 and experiment 5.

Mr of Na2CO3.nH2O = 14.3/0.0412 = 347 (3 s.f.)
A1
Mr of nH2O = 347 - 106 = 241; n = 241/18 = 13.4, rounds to n = 13
B1
0.00206 mol (3 s.f.) -> 0.00103 mol (3 s.f.) -> 0.0412 mol/dm3 (3 s.f.)
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
B1
Phenolphthalein changes colour at a higher pH (8.0-9.8) than bromophenol blue (3.0-4.6), so the titration would be stopped earlier, giving a smaller volume of P than the true end-point; the amount of HCl -- and hence the amount of Na2CO3 -- calculated would therefore be smaller than expected.
B2
Because a smaller amount of Na2CO3 is calculated, the Mr of the hydrate obtained is too large, so the value of n calculated would be larger than expected.
PART (E)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Some CO2 gas escapes from the boiling tube in the time taken to add solid Y and replace the bung (with its delivery tube), before the tube is resealed.
PART (E)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
Suspend a small test-tube containing Y on a thread inside the boiling tube (tipping it in once sealed), or add Y via a dropping/thistle funnel through the bung, so the solid can be added without removing the bung.

Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to solid Y and the mixture is warmed; a colourless gas that turns moist red litmus blue is evolved.
An acidified aqueous solution of Y reacts with aqueous potassium iodide to form iodine.
When solid Y is heated, only V2O5, water and gas Z are formed.
PART (A) · 3 MARKS
Determine the empirical formula of compound Y from the percentage composition by mass (H 3.4%, N 12.0%, O 41.0%, V 43.6%)

Suggest one property of aqueous Y caused by the presence of vanadium

Deduce the formula of each of the two ions present in Y

Draw it
PART (D) · 2 MARKS
State and explain what can be deduced about the redox nature of Y from its reaction with acidified aqueous potassium iodide to form iodine
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E)(I) · 1 MARK
Name gas Z, formed along with V2O5 and water when solid Y is heated

Write an equation for the thermal decomposition of Y (NH4VO3) to V2O5, water and ammonia

questions.question:
Malic acid is a carboxylic acid found in apple juice.
The equation for the reaction between malic acid, H2C4H4O5, and aqueous potassium hydroxide, KOH, is: 2KOH + H2C4H4O5 -> K2C4H4O5 + 2H2O.
The concentration of aqueous malic acid (P, apple juice) is determined by titration against Q, 0.0500 mol/dm3 KOH(aq), using thymolphthalein indicator I (end-point = solution remains colourless for at least 30 s).
Candidates titrate P into Q, record burette readings and observations, select best (concordant) results, calculate the average volume of P used, the moles of KOH, the moles of malic acid (2:1 KOH:acid ratio) and the concentration of malic acid in P, then suggest why the titration-derived value is usually higher than the true value.
Candidates are also given a copper(II) salt R and: (Test 1) perform a flame test on a wet wooden splint dipped in R; (Test 2) dissolve R in dilute nitric acid then add solid sodium chloride; (Test 3) dilute the Test 2 solution with water and observe; then identify a positive confirmatory test for the anion present, and explain why dilute nitric acid was added in Test 2.
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
From the titration results, obtain and show the average volume of P used (from the best/concordant titrations selected in (a)(i)).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
Calculate the number of moles of aqueous KOH in 25.0 cm3 of Q (0.0500 mol/dm3).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 1 MARK
Use the answer from (b)(i) to calculate the number of moles of malic acid, H2C4H4O5, in the average volume of P used.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(III) · 1 MARK
Use the answer from (b)(ii) to calculate the concentration (mol/dm3) of malic acid in P.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 1 MARK
Suggest why the accurate titration of apple juice with aqueous KOH usually produces an average value higher than the calculated answer from (b)(iii).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(I) · 4 MARKS
Carry out and record observations for three tests on copper(II) salt R: Test 1 (flame test on a wet splint dipped in R), Test 2 (dissolve R in dilute nitric acid, then add solid sodium chloride), Test 3 (dilute the Test 2 mixture with water).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(II) · 2 MARKS
Describe a positive confirmatory test to identify the anion present in the solution obtained in Test 3, carry it out, and record the observation.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D)(III) · 1 MARK
Explain why dilute nitric acid was added to salt R in Test 2.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
A1
average volume of P = (13.70 + 13.90)/2 = 13.80 cm3
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
A1
moles KOH = 0.0500 x (25.0/1000) = 0.00125 mol
PART (B)(II) · 1 MARK
A1
moles malic acid = 1/2 x 0.00125 = 0.000625 mol
PART (B)(III) · 1 MARK
A1
concentration = 0.000625 / (13.80/1000) = 0.000625/0.01380 = 0.0453 mol/dm3 (3 s.f.)
PART (C) · 1 MARK
B1
Apple juice contains other acids besides malic acid; these are also neutralised by the KOH, so more KOH is needed and the calculated concentration is higher than the true malic acid concentration.
PART (D)(I) · 4 MARKS
B1
Test 1: a green/blue-green flame is observed.
B2
Test 2: R dissolves in dilute nitric acid to form a blue solution.
B3
On adding solid sodium chloride, the blue solution turns green.
B4
On adding water, the green solution turns back to blue.
PART (D)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
Add dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate.
B2
A white precipitate is formed, confirming Cl- is present.
PART (D)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
To remove any carbonate ions that might be present in salt R, so they do not interfere with the later test for the anion.
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
Sulfamic acid, HA, is present in a cleaning product.
P is 0.200 mol/dm3 aqueous NaOH; Q is aqueous sulfamic acid made by diluting 100 cm3 of the cleaning product to 1.00 dm3 with deionised water; T is thymolphthalein indicator.
Titrate 25.0 cm3 of Q (pipetted into a conical flask, few drops of T added) against P from the burette to a permanent faint blue end-point.
HA + NaOH -> NaA + H2O.
Use the results to find the concentration of sulfamic acid in the cleaning product.
Separately, the Mr of sulfamic acid is found by reacting solid HA with excess aqueous sodium carbonate and collecting the CO2 evolved by downward displacement of water: 2HA + Na2CO3 -> CO2 + H2O + 2NaA.
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
From your titration results, show how you obtained the average volume of P used.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
Using your average volume of P from (a)(ii) and the equation HA + NaOH -> NaA + H2O, calculate the number of moles of sulfamic acid, HA, present in 25.0 cm3 of Q.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm3, of sulfamic acid in the cleaning product.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(I) · 5 MARKS
Outline a method, using gas collection by downward displacement of water, to determine the Mr of sulfamic acid, HA, by reacting a known mass of solid HA with excess aqueous sodium carbonate (2HA + Na2CO3 -> CO2 + H2O + 2NaA). State the apparatus used, the measurements taken, and how the results would be used to calculate the Mr of HA.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(II) · 3 MARKS
Carbon dioxide is soluble in water. Suggest how this may cause the calculated Mr of sulfamic acid to differ from its theoretical value. Explain your answer.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(III) · 1 MARK
Suggest and explain one change to the experiment that would improve the accuracy of the calculated Mr.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
A1
average volume of P = (18.90 + 18.90)/2 = 18.90 cm3 (the rough titre of 18.70 cm3 is excluded as it is not concordant with the other two)
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
M1
moles of NaOH = 0.200 x (18.90/1000) = 0.00378 mol; since HA : NaOH = 1 : 1, moles of HA = 0.00378 mol
PART (B)(II) · 2 MARKS
M1
moles of HA in 1.00 dm3 of Q = 0.00378 x (1000/25.0) = 0.1512 mol; concentration of HA in the cleaning product = 0.1512 / (100/1000) = 1.51 mol/dm3
A1
concentration of sulfamic acid in the cleaning product = 1.51 mol/dm3
PART (C)(I) · 5 MARKS
B1
Apparatus: a measuring cylinder to measure the aqueous sodium carbonate, and an electronic balance to weigh the solid HA.
B2
The aqueous sodium carbonate is used in excess, so that all the solid HA reacts.
B3
Record the total volume of CO2 collected (by downward displacement of water) once effervescence has stopped and the volume no longer changes.
B4
moles of CO2 = volume of CO2 / 24000; from 2HA : 1CO2, moles of HA = 2 x moles of CO2
B5
Mr of HA = mass of HA used / moles of HA calculated
PART (C)(II) · 3 MARKS
B1
Some of the CO2 dissolves in the water, so the volume of CO2 collected is lower than the actual volume produced.
B2
The calculated number of moles of CO2, and hence the calculated number of moles of HA, will be lower than the true value.
B3
As a result, the calculated Mr of HA will be larger than the true/theoretical value.
PART (C)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
Use a gas syringe to collect the CO2 (instead of downward displacement of water), so the measured volume equals the true volume produced, since none of the gas is lost to dissolving in water.
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
Nitrous oxide, N2O, is used as a propellant in aerosol whipped-cream cans.
Ammonium nitrate, NH4NO3, is heated gently to decompose to N2O and water (NH4NO3 -> N2O + 2H2O). 4.40 g of NH4NO3 was used.
PART (A)(I) · 2 MARKS
Calculate the mass of N2O produced.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
Determine the percent yield if 2.50 g of N2O was actually produced.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
Explain the (>100%) yield determined in (a)(ii)
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
N2O is occasionally injected into racing-car engines for extra power; N2O decomposes exothermically to N2 and O2. Propose two ways the introduction of N2O provides an extra boost to engine power.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 2 MARKS
M1
moles NH4NO3 = 4.40 / 80 = 0.0550 mol; moles N2O = 0.0550 mol (1 : 1 ratio in the equation)
A1
mass of N2O = 0.0550 mol x 44 g/mol = 2.42 g
PART (A)(II) · 1 MARK
A1
% yield = (2.50 / 2.42) x 100% = 103.3%
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
the N2O collected/product was impure — impurities present in it added to the measured mass, making the yield appear greater than 100%
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
decomposition of N2O releases (additional) O2, which reacts with more fuel during combustion, releasing more energy
B2
the decomposition of N2O to N2 and O2 is exothermic, releasing heat energy which is transferred to/gained by the engine
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
Determination of the relative formula mass of barium peroxide, BaO2, by iodometric titration.
Solution R (containing hydrogen peroxide) was prepared by adding dilute sulfuric acid to 8.50 g of barium peroxide, filtering off insoluble barium sulfate, and diluting the resulting solution to 1.00 dm3: BaO2(s) + H2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + H2O2(aq) [equation 1].
The concentration of hydrogen peroxide in R is determined by adding acidified aqueous potassium iodide and titrating the liberated iodine with aqueous sodium thiosulfate: H2O2 + 2KI + 2H+ -> I2 + 2H2O + 2K+ [equation 2]; I2 + 2Na2S2O3 -> 2NaI + Na2S4O6 [equation 3].
Q is 0.100 mol/dm3 sodium thiosulfate.
PART (B) · 1 MARK
From the titration results, obtain and show working for the average volume of Q used.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 1 MARK
Use equation 3 to calculate the number of moles of iodine liberated.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D) · 2 MARKS
Using the answer from (c) and equation 2, calculate the concentration of hydrogen peroxide in R, in mol/dm3.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
Using the answer to (d), calculate the relative formula mass of barium peroxide.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (F) · 2 MARKS
State and explain the impact on the titration results of a student not rinsing the burette with Q (rinsed only with distilled water) before performing the titration.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (G) · 2 MARKS
Using oxidation numbers, show that equation 2 (H2O2 + 2KI + 2H+ -> I2 + 2H2O + 2K+) is a redox reaction.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (B) · 1 MARK
M1
Average volume of Q = mean of the concordant titres, with working shown, e.g. (25.10 + 25.10)/2 = 25.10 cm3, quoted to 2 d.p.
PART (C) · 1 MARK
M1
moles Na2S2O3 = (25.20/1000) x 0.100 = 0.00252 mol; moles I2 = 1/2 x 0.00252 = 0.00126 mol
PART (D) · 2 MARKS
M1
moles H2O2 (in 25.0 cm3 of R) = moles I2 (1:1 ratio) = 0.00126 mol
A1
concentration of H2O2 = 0.00126 / (25.0/1000) = 0.0504 mol/dm3
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
M1
moles BaO2 in 1.00 dm3 = 0.0504 mol (1:1 with H2O2); Mr = 8.50 / 0.0504
A1
Mr of BaO2 = 8.50 / 0.0504 = 169 (3 s.f.)
PART (F) · 2 MARKS
B1
The residual distilled water dilutes Q, lowering its concentration.
B2
A larger volume of the more dilute Q is needed to react with the same amount of iodine, so the titre obtained is larger than expected.
PART (G) · 2 MARKS
B1
Oxidation number of iodine increases from -1 (in KI) to 0 (in I2); KI is oxidised.
B2
Oxidation number of oxygen decreases from -1 (in H2O2) to -2 (in H2O); H2O2 is reduced.
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
Four 2.00 g samples of metal carbonates (calcium carbonate, copper(II) carbonate, magnesium carbonate, zinc carbonate) are heated strongly until there is no further change in mass. Table 6.1 gives mass remaining after heating: CaCO3 1.12 g, CuCO3 1.29 g, MgCO3 0.95 g, ZnCO3 1.35 g.
PART (A) · 3 MARKS
Calculate the percentage yield of carbon dioxide formed when 2.00 g of zinc carbonate is heated.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 1 MARK
Explain why the mass of carbon dioxide formed is different for each metal carbonate.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
Hydrogen was passed over heated aluminium oxide and heated copper(II) oxide in two separate experiments. Describe the observation, if any, expected in each experiment, and explain your reasoning.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 3 MARKS
M1
ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2; Mr(ZnCO3) = 125; n(ZnCO3) = 2.00/125 = 0.016 mol; theoretical mass CO2 = 0.016 x 44 = 0.704 g
M2
actual mass of CO2 = 2.00 - 1.35 = 0.65 g
A1
% yield = (0.65/0.704) x 100% = 92.3% (3 s.f.)
PART (B) · 1 MARK
B1
Different Mr for each carbonate means the fixed 2.00 g sample contains a different number of moles of carbonate, hence a different mass of CO2 is released
B2
Different Ar of the metal in each carbonate means the fixed 2.00 g sample contains a different number of moles of carbonate, hence a different mass of CO2 is released
B3
Different % of carbon in each compound means the fixed 2.00 g sample contains a different number of moles of carbonate, hence a different mass of CO2 is released
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
B1
No change with Al2O3; CuO (black) turns pink/red-brown as Cu metal forms
B2
H2 is less reactive than Al, so cannot reduce Al2O3; H2 is more reactive than Cu, so reduces CuO to Cu
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
Part 1: Bleach solution Q contains the oxidising agent chlorate(I) ion, which liberates iodine from acidified aqueous potassium iodide; the iodine liberated is titrated with aqueous sodium thiosulfate R (0.0500 mol/dm3) using starch indicator, to determine the concentration of chlorate(I) ions in the original commercial bleach (Q was prepared by diluting 100 cm3 of commercial bleach to 1.00 dm3).

Part 2: solution T is tested with aqueous potassium iodide to identify its nature via any gas evolved.
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
In the titration, the average volume of aqueous sodium thiosulfate R (0.0500 mol/dm3) needed to react with the iodine liberated from a 25.0 cm3 sample of solution Q was found to be 21.00 cm3. Calculate the number of moles of aqueous sodium thiosulfate used in the titration.

Two moles of aqueous sodium thiosulfate react with one mole of iodine (2S2O32- + I2 -> S4O62- + 2I-). Using your answer to (b)(i), calculate the number of moles of iodine liberated in the reaction.

One mole of chlorate(I) ions liberates one mole of iodine (ClO- + 2I- + 2H+ -> Cl- + I2 + H2O). Using your answer to (b)(ii), calculate the number of moles of chlorate(I) ions present in the 25.0 cm3 sample of solution Q used in the titration.

Solution Q was prepared by diluting 100 cm3 of the original commercial bleach to 1.00 dm3 with water. Using your answer to (b)(iii), calculate the concentration, in mol/dm3, of chlorate(I) ions in the original commercial bleach. Show clearly how you scale from the 25.0 cm3 sample of Q to the whole of Q, and then to the original 100 cm3 of commercial bleach, and give your final answer to an appropriate number of significant figures with its unit.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C)(I) · 2 MARKS
1 cm depth of aqueous potassium iodide is added to solution T and the mixture is shaken. State what you would observe, and describe the test and result you would use to identify any gas evolved.
Attach photo or sketch

PART (C)(II) · 1 MARK
What can be deduced about the nature of solution T?

questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
M1
no. of mol of Na2S2O3 = 0.0500 x (21.00/1000) = 1.05 x 10^-3 mol (0.00105 mol)
PART (B)(II) · 1 MARK
M1
no. of mol of I2 = 1/2 x 0.00105 = 5.25 x 10^-4 mol (0.000525 mol)
PART (B)(III) · 1 MARK
M1
no. of mol of ClO- in 25.0 cm3 of Q = 5.25 x 10^-4 mol (same as moles of I2)
PART (B)(IV) · 4 MARKS

no. of mol of ClO- in 1000 cm3 of Q = 5.25 x 10^-4 x (1000/25) = 0.0210 mol

no. of mol of ClO- in the original 100 cm3 of commercial bleach = 0.0210 mol (same as in 1000 cm3 of Q); concentration of ClO- in commercial bleach = 0.0210 x (1000/100) = 0.210 mol/dm3
A1
0.210 mol/dm3 (3 s.f.)
A2
unit: mol/dm3
PART (C)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
the colourless solution turns yellowish-brown (brown)
B2
effervescence is seen; the gas relights a glowing splint; the gas is oxygen
PART (C)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
solution T contains an oxidising agent

questions.question:
Methane, CH4, is a commonly used gas for household cooking (colourless, odourless, burns with a bright blue flame). 20 cm3 of methane and 60 cm3 of oxygen are reacted to form carbon dioxide and water as the only products, at room temperature and pressure.
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
Write a balanced chemical equation with state symbols for the reaction of methane and oxygen.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 3 MARKS
Determine which is the limiting reagent for the reaction of 20 cm3 methane with 60 cm3 oxygen.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 2 MARKS
Calculate the total volume of gas remaining at the end of the reaction at room temperature and pressure.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D) · 1 MARK
In reality, the percentage yield of carbon dioxide produced is only 70%. Calculate the volume of CO2 produced.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
B1
CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O
B2
CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)

M1
Mole/volume ratio CH4 : O2 = 1 : 2; volume of O2 required = 20 x 2 = 40 cm3

O2 available (60 cm3) > O2 required (40 cm3), so O2 is in excess

Vol CO2 produced = 20 cm3 (CH4:CO2 = 1:1); Vol O2 remaining = 60 - 40 = 20 cm3
A1
Total volume of gas remaining = 20.0 (CO2) + 20.0 (O2 excess) = 40.0 cm3

A1
Actual volume of CO2 = 70/100 x 20 = 14.0 cm3

questions.question:
The percentage purity of Na2CO3 can be determined by titration as described in question 1 (Na2CO3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)). Based on the equation above, suggest another way to determine the percentage purity of sodium carbonate in the impure sample.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 5 MARKS
B1
Add excess dilute HCl to 25.0 cm3 of solution P in a conical flask and either collect the CO2 gas evolved using a gas syringe (recording the final volume when no further change occurs), or place the flask on a balance (plugged loosely with cotton wool) and record the loss in mass once effervescence stops.
B2
moles of CO2 = volume of CO2 (cm3) / 24000, OR moles of CO2 = mass of CO2 lost (g) / 44.
B3
From the equation, mole ratio Na2CO3 : CO2 = 1 : 1, so moles of Na2CO3 in 25.0 cm3 of P = moles of CO2 found.
B4
mass of Na2CO3 in 25.0 cm3 = moles of Na2CO3 x 106; mass of Na2CO3 in 1.00 dm3 of P = mass in 25.0 cm3 x (1000/25).
B5
% purity = (mass of Na2CO3 in 1.00 dm3 of P / 6.00) x 100%.
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with dilute nitric acid: Mg + 2HNO3 -> Mg(NO3)2 + H2.
Fig. 8.1 shows two graphs (reaction A and reaction B) of loss in mass vs time when Mg reacts with dilute nitric acid, with the beaker and contents weighed every two minutes.
In reaction A, 1.20 g of magnesium was added to 250 cm3 of dilute nitric acid of 0.500 mol/dm3.
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
State the reason for the loss in mass in reaction A.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 3 MARKS
With the aid of calculations, determine the limiting reactant.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 1 MARK
State the change made to the experiment to produce the graph for reaction B in Fig. 8.1.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
A third reaction, C, is repeated with the addition of 50 cm3 of aqueous copper(II) sulfate. A student predicted: 'The loss in mass is lower as the aqueous copper(II) sulfate reacts with one of the reactants.' Do you agree with this statement? Explain your reasoning.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
Hydrogen gas (H2), produced as the magnesium reacts with the acid, escapes into the atmosphere, so the total mass of the beaker and its contents decreases over time.
PART (A)(II) · 3 MARKS
M1
n(Mg) = 1.20/24 = 0.05 mol; n(HNO3) = 0.500 mol/dm3 x 0.250 dm3 = 0.125 mol
M2
Mole ratio Mg : HNO3 = 1 : 2, so 0.05 mol Mg requires 2 x 0.05 = 0.100 mol HNO3.
A1
0.125 mol HNO3 available > 0.100 mol HNO3 required, so HNO3 is in excess and Mg is the limiting reagent.
PART (B) · 1 MARK
B1
A lower temperature was used for reaction B (than for reaction A).
B2
Larger lumps of magnesium (smaller surface area) were used instead of the magnesium used in reaction A.
B3
A lower concentration of nitric acid was used for reaction B, with the acid still in excess.
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
B1
I agree with the student's statement.
B2
Magnesium is more reactive than copper, so magnesium displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution (a displacement reaction occurs).
B3
As a result, less magnesium is left to react with the nitric acid, so less hydrogen gas is produced, and less loss in mass occurs.
This question is not counting towards your marks. Anything you already earned is kept.

questions.question:
A student was given a sample of a metal hydroxide of formula B(OH)2 and asked to identify element B by titrating an aqueous solution of B(OH)2 with 0.095 mol/dm3 nitric acid. questions.question:
Fig B7.1 shows Mendeleev's 1869 Periodic Table (elements arranged by increasing relative atomic mass).
Graph B7.2 plots atomic radius (nm) vs atomic number for successive periods in the modern Periodic Table.
Atomic radius is determined by nuclear attraction and screening by inner-shell electrons.
PART (A) · 3 MARKS
Describe three differences between Mendeleev's Periodic Table and the modern Periodic Table.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 1 MARK
What is the current symbol of the element on the modern Periodic Table represented by J on Mendeleev's?
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 1 MARK
With reference to Mendeleev's table, give one example of 'a reactive non-metal followed by a reactive light metal then a less reactive light metal'.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (D) · 3 MARKS
Describe the trend in atomic radii across period 2 and 3, and explain the trend.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E) · 3 MARKS
A student states: 'The reactivity of Group I metals and halogens is closely related to the trend of atomic radii for these elements.' Do you support her statement? Explain your reasoning.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (F) · 1 MARK
In period 4 and subsequent periods, the trend in atomic radii is interrupted by certain elements. What are these elements?
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 3 MARKS
B1
Mendeleev's table is arranged in order of increasing relative atomic mass; the modern Periodic Table is arranged in order of increasing atomic (proton) number.
B2
Mendeleev's table does not include the noble gases (Group 0/18), which had not yet been discovered; the modern table includes them.
B3
In the modern table the transition elements are shown as a separate block; in Mendeleev's table they were listed together with the main group elements.
B4
The modern Periodic Table has around 114 (now over 118) elements, compared with only about 60 known in Mendeleev's time.
B5
Mendeleev left gaps for elements not yet discovered; most of these gaps have since been filled by newly discovered elements in the modern table.
B6
Except for Group II elements, elements belonging to the same period in the modern table occur in the same column of Mendeleev's table.
PART (B) · 1 MARK
B1
I (iodine)
PART (C) · 1 MARK
B1
F, Na, Mg (or Cl, K, Ca)
PART (D) · 3 MARKS
B1
Atomic radius decreases across period 2 and period 3 (from left to right).
B2
Across the period, the atomic (proton) number increases, so the attraction of the nucleus for the outer electrons increases.
B3
The amount of screening/shielding by inner shells remains the same across the period, as the number of inner shells does not change.
PART (E) · 3 MARKS
B1
Agree - down each group (Group I and Group VII/halogens), atomic radius increases (more electron shells are added), which affects the attraction of the nucleus for the outer electron.
B2
Down Group I, it becomes easier to lose the outer electron to form a positive ion (as the atom gets bigger and attraction weakens), so the reactivity of the alkali metals increases down the group.
B3
Down Group VII, it becomes harder to gain an additional electron to form a negative ion (as the atom gets bigger and attraction weakens), so the reactivity of the halogens decreases down the group.
PART (F) · 1 MARK
B1
Transition elements (transition metals).

questions.question:
Fig. 4.1 shows selected elements from Groups 1, 2, 13-18 of Periods 2-5 (Li, C, O, F; Na, Cl; K, Br; Rb, I). Table 4.1 gives melting point and electrical conductivity data for lithium, carbon (graphite) and oxygen (all Period 2).
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
For each of four statements about periodic trends, state True or False: (1) atoms lose electrons more easily down Group 1; (2) melting point decreases from fluorine to iodine; (3) the strongest non-metal oxidising agent is at the top of a group; (4) metallic character increases across Period 3.

Draw it

Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 2 MARKS
B1
True
B2
False — melting point increases down Group 17 (F to I) as van der Waals forces strengthen with increasing molecular size / number of electrons
B3
True
B4
False — metallic character decreases across a period
PART (B) · 5 MARKS
B1
Lithium has a giant metallic structure; graphite has a giant covalent (giant molecular) structure; oxygen has a simple molecular structure.
B2
Lithium: strong electrostatic attraction between Li+ ions and delocalised (sea of) electrons. Graphite: strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms. Oxygen: weak intermolecular / van der Waals forces between O2 molecules.
B3
Graphite has the highest melting point because a lot of energy is needed to break the strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms; oxygen has the lowest melting point because only a little energy is needed to overcome the weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
B4
Lithium conducts because the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge. Oxygen does not conduct because it has no mobile ions or free electrons to carry charge.
B5
Each carbon atom in graphite is bonded to only 3 other carbon atoms, leaving 1 delocalised electron per atom; these free electrons move through the structure and conduct electricity.

questions.question:
Two solids XCO3 and YCO3 are Group 2 metal carbonates.
Group 2 carbonates decompose on heating to form metal oxide and carbon dioxide: metal carbonate -> metal oxide + carbon dioxide.
Given 1 g of each carbonate, outline a method (using only apparatus/reagents normally found in a school laboratory) involving this reaction to determine which of the two metals, X or Y, has the higher relative atomic mass (Ar: C = 12, O = 16).
The method should state the measurements taken and explain how the results would be used to determine which metal has the higher Ar.
PART (PROCEDURE) · 2 MARKS
Describe the procedure, including apparatus and measurements taken, for determining which metal (X or Y) has the higher relative atomic mass by thermal decomposition of the carbonates. (Any ONE of the three valid routes: mass-loss-to-constant-mass, gas-volume-to-constant-volume, or rate/fixed-time-or-volume.)
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (TREATMENT)(OF)(RESULTS) · 2 MARKS
Explain how the measurements would be used (treatment of results) to determine which metal, X or Y, has the higher relative atomic mass. (Must be consistent with whichever of the three routes was chosen: mass-ratio algebra, gas-volume comparison, or thermal-stability/rate comparison.)
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (PROCEDURE) · 2 MARKS
B1
Weigh 1 g of each carbonate accurately using an electronic balance before heating; after heating, cool and reweigh the solid residue.
B2
Continue to heat, cool and reweigh the residue until two consecutive readings are the same, i.e. a constant mass is obtained.
B3
Connect the boiling tube containing the carbonate to a gas syringe and heat strongly; collect the carbon dioxide gas produced in the gas syringe.
B4
Continue heating until the reading on the gas syringe no longer increases, i.e. a constant volume of gas has been collected.
B5
Start timing as soon as heating begins; record the volume of gas collected in the gas syringe after a fixed time, e.g. 2 minutes (or record the time taken to collect a fixed volume of gas, e.g. 10 cm3).
PART (TREATMENT)(OF)(RESULTS) · 2 MARKS
B1
Since 1 mol of MCO3 forms 1 mol of MO, moles of carbonate = moles of oxide. Using moles = mass/Mr, set mass of carbonate/(Ar+60) = mass of oxide/(Ar+16) for each metal and solve for Ar of X and Ar of Y.
B2
Compare the Ar values obtained: the metal giving the larger Ar is the answer. Equivalently, %mass decrease = 44/(Ar+60) x 100%, so the carbonate showing the SMALLER percentage decrease in mass contains the metal with the higher Ar.
B3
Moles of CO2 produced = moles of carbonate reacted (1:1 mole ratio). Since moles = mass/Mr and the starting masses are equal, the carbonate with the larger Mr (higher Ar metal) has fewer moles reacting, producing a smaller volume of CO2.
B4
For the same starting mass, the carbonate producing the SMALLER volume of CO2 has fewer moles reacting, so it has the larger molar mass and hence the metal with the HIGHER Ar.
B5
Down Group 2, as Ar increases, the carbonates become more thermally stable / harder to decompose on heating.
B6
The carbonate that produces less CO2 in the fixed time (or takes longer to produce the fixed volume of gas) decomposes more slowly, i.e. is more thermally stable, so it contains the metal with the HIGHER Ar.

questions.question:
A factory is suspected of releasing calcium, aluminium, zinc and nitrate ions into a river. A scientist tested two river-water samples by adding aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia respectively, then warming with aluminium foil (Table 9): NaOH -- few drops: white ppt; excess: white ppt soluble in excess giving colourless solution; warming with Al foil: no visible reaction. Aqueous ammonia -- few drops: white ppt; excess: white ppt, SOME soluble in excess giving colourless solution, some remained insoluble; warming with Al foil: gas evolved turns damp litmus paper blue. The scientist claimed Al3+, Zn2+ and NO3- were all present; the factory owner argued only Al3+ and Zn2+ were shown, not NO3-.
PART (A)(I) · 3 MARKS
Explain how the data shows calcium ions are absent but both aluminium and zinc ions are present.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
The scientist claims nitrate ions are detected because the ammonia test produced ammonia gas -- do you agree? Explain.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (B) · 2 MARKS

Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 3 MARKS

Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A)(I) · 3 MARKS
B1
The white precipitate formed with NaOH dissolves completely in excess to give a colourless solution; if Ca2+ were present, Ca(OH)2 (insoluble in excess NaOH) would remain as a residue, so calcium ions are absent.
B2
With aqueous ammonia, part of the precipitate dissolves in excess ammonia (Zn(OH)2 dissolves to form a soluble complex), so zinc ions are present.
B3
With aqueous ammonia, part of the precipitate remains undissolved even in excess (Al(OH)3 does not dissolve in excess ammonia), so aluminium ions are present.
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
B1
No, I do not agree -- the ammonia gas evolved could just be from the aqueous ammonia already present in the sample/reagent, not from nitrate being reduced by the aluminium foil.
B2
To properly test for nitrate ions, warm aqueous sodium hydroxide (not aqueous ammonia) should be used with aluminium foil, since aqueous ammonia already contains ammonia and would give a false/ambiguous positive.
PART (B) · 2 MARKS
B1
Add dilute nitric acid to the water sample, followed by aqueous silver nitrate.
B2
A white precipitate (AgCl) forms if chloride ions are present.
PART (C) · 3 MARKS
B1
Add excess zinc carbonate powder to warm dilute hydrochloric acid, a little at a time, until no more dissolves/reacts (effervescence stops).
B2
Filter the mixture to remove the excess (unreacted) zinc carbonate; heat the filtrate to the point of saturation (a hot saturated solution).
B3
Allow the hot saturated solution to cool so that zinc chloride crystals form; filter off the crystals, wash with a little distilled water, and dry between pieces of filter paper.

B1

3 : 2 (phosphoric acid : tartaric acid), since H3PO4 has 3 replaceable/ionisable H+ per molecule while tartaric acid has 2.

B1
6.0 degC — because magnesium is the limiting reactant in both reactions (the same amount of Mg reacts each time), the same quantity of heat energy is released, so the temperature change is unchanged.

6.0 degC; magnesium is the limiting reactant in both cases (the same 2.0 cm length of Mg is used each time), so the same number of moles of Mg reacts and releases the same quantity of heat energy — hence the same temperature change.

B2
Mg + H3PO4 (reactants, higher energy) -> magnesium phosphate + H2 (products, lower energy); vertical drop from reactants to products labelled 'enthalpy change of reaction' (exothermic); rise from reactants level up to the peak of the curve labelled 'activation energy'.

questions.question:
Manganese ores from four mines are given in Table 7.1: Alpha (5–9% ore, pyrolusite, MnO2), Beta (2–12% ore, manganite, MnO(OH)), Gamma (8–13% ore, hausmannite, Mn3O4), Delta (1–4% ore, rhodochrosite, MnCO3).
Extraction: manganese is extracted by smelting the ores in a blast furnace — higher oxides (Mn2O3, MnO2) are reduced to MnO by carbon monoxide; MnO is reduced to the metal only at elevated temperature by carbon.
Silica in the ores combines with MnO and prevents its reduction; this is overcome by roasting limestone with the ores, though this produces more slag (dissolving some manganese) and can reduce silica to silicon which enters the molten metal — giving a metal of 65–80% manganese purity.
Purification: the ores are roasted to MnO, dissolved in dilute sulfuric acid to form raw manganese(II) sulfate solution; aqueous ammonia precipitates out iron(III) and aluminium ions; aqueous hydrogen sulfide precipitates out cobalt, copper, lead and zinc; the purified solution is electrolysed using stainless steel and graphite electrodes (Fig. 7.1) — the electrolyte must be replaced periodically or effervescence at the cathode intensifies.
Deposited manganese flakes are heated to 500°C to remove hydrogen gas, giving >99.9% purity manganese.

Draw it

Draw it

M2

B1
Since the minimum possible mass of Mn from Gamma (0.0576 t) is still greater than the maximum possible mass of Mn from Alpha (0.0569 t), Gamma always produces more manganese than Alpha, whatever the actual percentages turn out to be.

B1

H+ ions are discharged (reduced) at the cathode to form hydrogen gas, which becomes trapped between/within the deposited manganese flakes.

questions.question:
A student was tasked to obtain sugar from a mixture of salt and sugar.
Sugar is soluble in both water and ethanol; salt is soluble in water but insoluble in ethanol.
The student's written procedure was: 1.
Add water to the sugar and salt mixture and stir. 2.
Filter the mixture. 3.
Heat the filtrate till it is saturated. 4.
Leave it to cool and crystallise. 5.
Filter to collect the crystals. 6.
Wash the crystals with warm distilled water to remove impurities.

questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT

B1
Step 1 is wrong: water dissolves both salt and sugar (salt is also soluble in water), so filtration cannot separate them. Rectification: use ethanol instead of water, since sugar is soluble in ethanol but salt is not, so the undissolved salt can be filtered off as residue.

B1
At a higher temperature, the perfume particles gain more kinetic energy and move faster.
B2
They therefore diffuse at a faster rate, from the region of higher concentration (near the teacher) to the region of lower concentration (other parts of the classroom), so the smell is detected sooner.

Set up a conical flask connected by a delivery tube to an inverted measuring cylinder that is completely filled with water and standing in a trough of water, so that CO2 gas is collected by downward displacement of water. Weigh the solid Na2CO3 on an electronic balance.
B2
Measure a known volume of vinegar (e.g. 25 cm3) using a measuring cylinder and place it in a conical flask. Admontite MgB6O10.7H2O has alternative formula MgB6Ox(OH)6.yH2O; state x and y.

Draw it

Draw it

Attach photo or sketch
Draw it

questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (A) · 1 MARK
B1
The average mass of one atom of an element relative to 1/12 the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
A1
24.3 = 24x + 25(0.10) + 26(0.90 - x) => x = 0.80, so Mg-24 = 80%
PART (B)(II) · 1 MARK
A1
Mg-26 = 90% - 80% = 10%
PART (C) · 1 MARK
B1
Mg-24 diffuses fastest, Mg-25 diffuses at an intermediate rate, and Mg-26 diffuses slowest, since rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass.
PART (D) · 2 MARKS
M1
n(Mg) = 18.9/24 = 0.7875 mol; n(B) = 5.8/11 = 0.527 mol; n(O) = 25.3/16 = 1.581 mol

Mg : B : O = 0.7875/0.527 : 0.527/0.527 : 1.581/0.527 = 1.5 : 1 : 3 = 3 : 2 : 6, so empirical formula is Mg3B2O6
PART (E) · 1 MARK
B1
Total O in MgB6O10.7H2O = 10 + 7 = 17; (OH)6 accounts for 6 O and 6 H; total H = 14 (from 7H2O), so 2y = 14 - 6 = 8, y = 4; x = 17 - 6 - 4 = 7. So x = 7, y = 4.

questions.answer:

B1
Nucleon number = 18 + 22 = 40; electronic configuration = 2,8,8

B1
R has a stable electronic configuration with a full octet (8 electrons) in its outermost shell, making it inert/unreactive, so it exists as single atoms.

Upper bound = 50000/114 = 438.6; range of average number of repeat units = 176 to 439 (whole numbers of repeat units).

B1

questions.question:

Explain how the equations show that chlorine atoms act as a catalyst for the breakdown of ozone.

Draw the structure of the monomer used to make polyvinyl chloride (PVC).

questions.answer:

PART (A)(I) · 2 MARKS
B1
ozone absorbs/blocks UV radiation; less ozone means more UV radiation reaches the Earth's surface
B2
increased risk of skin cancer / sunburn / cataracts / premature ageing of the skin
PART (A)(II) · 2 MARKS
M1
Cl + O3 + ClO + O3 -> ClO + O2 + 2O2 + Cl, which cancels Cl and ClO on both sides to leave 2 O3 and 3 O2
A1
2 O3 -> 3 O2
PART (A)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
chlorine is used up in the first step but reformed/regenerated in the second step, so it is chemically unchanged (not consumed) overall

B1
35Cl: protons = 17, neutrons = 18, electrons = 17
B2
37Cl: protons = 17, neutrons = 20, electrons = 17
PART (B)(I) · 1 MARK
B1
CH2=CHCl (chloroethene / vinyl chloride), with the C=C double bond shown
PART (B)(II) · 1 MARK
B1
non-biodegradable plastics do not rot away, so they fill landfill sites, causing a shortage of space for waste disposal / visual pollution (an eyesore)

plastic waste in the sea gets stuck in animals' digestive systems / animals get entangled in it / mistake it for food, or floating plastic blocks light reaching organisms in the sea

burning PVC releases poisonous/toxic gas (e.g. hydrogen chloride, HCl), causing air pollution
PART (B)(III) · 1 MARK
B1
recycling plastics conserves crude oil, a finite (non-renewable) resource
B2
recycling uses less energy than manufacturing new plastic from crude oil
B3
recycling reduces carbon dioxide/greenhouse gas emissions compared with producing new plastic

questions.answer:

Plastics are made from non-renewable petroleum(-based) resources, so production is not environmentally sustainable.

questions.question:
Malic acid, H2C4H4O5, reacts with potassium hydroxide: 2KOH + H2C4H4O5 -> K2C4H4O5 + 2H2O.
P is aqueous malic acid (in burette); Q is 0.100 mol/dm3 KOH(aq), 25.0 cm3 pipetted into a conical flask and titrated with P using thymolphthalein indicator (end-point = solution remains colourless permanently).
Record titration results, determine average volume of P, then calculate:
(b)
moles of KOH in 25.0 cm3 of Q;
(c)
moles of malic acid in average volume of P;
(d)
concentration of malic acid in P; given average concentration of malic acid in apple juice = 4.50 g/dm3, (e) this concentration in mol/dm3 [Ar: H,1; C,12; O,16];
(f)
volume of apple juice containing the same mass of malic acid as 200 cm3 of P;
(g)
explain why real titration of apple juice with KOH usually gives a concentration higher than the answer to (e).
PART (B) · 1 MARK
Calculate the amount, in moles, of potassium hydroxide in 25.0 cm3 of Q (0.100 mol/dm3 KOH(aq)).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (C) · 1 MARK
Calculate the amount, in moles, of malic acid present in the average volume of P, using the mole ratio KOH : malic acid = 2 : 1.
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
Calculate the average concentration of malic acid in apple juice (given as 4.50 g/dm3) in mol/dm3. [Ar: H,1; C,12; O,16]
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
PART (G) · 1 MARK
Suggest why an accurate titration of apple juice with KOH usually gives an average concentration higher than the answer to (e).
Attach photo or sketch
Draw it
questions.answer:
THE ANSWER, POINT BY POINT
PART (B) · 1 MARK
A1
n(KOH) = c x V = 0.100 mol/dm3 x (25.0/1000) dm3 = 0.00250 mol (2.50 x 10^-3 mol)
PART (C) · 1 MARK
A1
n(malic acid) = n(KOH) / 2 = 0.00250 / 2 = 0.00125 mol (1.25 x 10^-3 mol)
PART (E) · 2 MARKS
M1
Mr(H2C4H4O5) = 2(1) + 4(12) + 4(1) + 5(16) = 2 + 48 + 4 + 80 = 134
A1
concentration = 4.50 g/dm3 / 134 g/mol = 0.033582... = 0.0336 mol/dm3
PART (G) · 1 MARK
B1
Apple juice contains other acids/acidic substances besides malic acid; these are also neutralised by the KOH, so the titration overestimates the malic acid concentration
